body:
Started as the stranger render-failure fixes and grew to cover the defect that was left open, plus three more the work exposed.

## ⚠️ Read before releasing to prod

**Deploy the prod renderer by hand BEFORE tagging a release.**

```
npm run deploy-ec2 -- i-0d6cc78fdfa124fdf --stage=prod    # instance must already be running
```

The backend now writes a payload pointer that only the new renderer can follow. `deploy-prod.yml` declares `deploy-processing: needs: deploy-backend`, so a tag deploys the backend first and the renderer after it, and every render started between the two jobs would fail. The renderer tolerates every older payload shape, so deploying it early is always safe. Recorded in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` under known CI gaps. Dev is already deployed in the right order.

## The original defect: a large project could not make a video

A stranger with 327 photos pressed "Make video" eight times. Every attempt died on the `PutItem` with `ValidationException: Item size has exceeded the maximum allowed size`. No `VIDEO#` record was written, so nothing in the product or the funnel recorded that anything had happened.

Measured on prod across 83 records before changing anything: cost scales with photos plus clips, not with top-level `videoItems` entries, at a median 1,134 bytes each. That puts the failure point between **277 and 361 items**, while a project can hold about **1,200 rows**. gzip was measured as the cheaper fix and rejected: at 76-83% of the limit it clears today and leaves room for nothing.

The payload now lives at `render-payloads/<projectId>/<videoId>.json` in the existing videos bucket. Write order is the object, then the `VIDEO_CONTENT#` sibling holding the pointer, then the `VIDEO#` record, so everything is written before anything that points at it. One write path, no size threshold; both older inline shapes are still read, so there is no migration.

**Proven end to end on dev**, not just in tests:

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Payload in S3 | 759,928 bytes, **1.85x what DynamoDB allowed** |
| `VIDEO_CONTENT#` row | 385 bytes, down from up to 400KB |
| Render | 450 items, 418MB mp4, ~6.5 minutes |
| Lambda memory | **229MB of 512** at 450 items, vs 252MB at 323 |

That memory number retires the concern that large projects would blow the 512MB ceiling. It is dominated by the Node runtime, not the payload.

All three delete paths were exercised against live records, including planting an orphan object to confirm the prefix sweep catches it.

## Four more defects, all found by that run

**Deleting a large project timed out and half-finished.** The cascade ran inside the request; at 450 photos that is ~1,350 external calls, past the 30s ceiling. API Gateway caps the HTTP API integration at 30s without a quota increase, so raising it was not available. `DELETE` now marks the project and answers **202**, and the cascade runs unchanged in a new `projectDeletionWorker` Lambda.

The mark REMOVEs the `UserProjectsIndex` keys rather than setting a flag the list filters on: that index is sparse, so the project leaves the owner's list at once at no read cost, and its INCLUDE projection cannot carry `status` because DynamoDB will not extend an existing GSI projection. `adminPk`/`adminSk` stay, so a project stranded by a dead worker is invisible to its owner but still findable by an operator. Project routes 404 a deleting project, checked once in `checkProjectOwnership`.

**The renderer could never call Rekognition.** No Rekognition permission in the instance role's inline policy or any of its eight managed policies, so `DetectFaces` returned AccessDenied on every render on both stages, logged at WARNING while the render continued. Face data drives the Ken Burns focus point and crop bounds. Grant applied by hand, since that role is not in IaC. The same path also wrote `face_data` where the backend reads `faceData`, so a success would have been discarded and re-billed next render. Both halves fixed.

**The delete sweep missed photo originals.** It swept `photos/<projectId>/` but the Google Photos import worker writes originals to `projects/<projectId>/photos/`. One dev project holds 778 objects under the unswept prefix.

**A frontend test leaked an async rejection past teardown.** `PhotoGallery.test.tsx` uses `vi.clearAllMocks()`, which clears calls but not implementations, so one test's `mockRejectedValue` survived into the next, which clicks delete and never awaits. Vitest counts that as an unhandled error and fails the run, so the suite failed roughly one run in three with no code change.

## Also in here, from the earlier session

- User-uploaded music made the video job unsaveable: `durationMs` in milliseconds vs `duration` in seconds produced a `NaN` and a 500 with no record. Three strangers blocked across 28 attempts; one pressed the button 14 times in an hour and filed "I press to make a video and it doesn t work".
- A 1-second credits slide drove the FFmpeg fade start to -0.50 and killed the render.
- The funnel counted a founder's own account as a stranger.

## Not covered, logged rather than dropped

The admin delete-user route loops the same cascade over every project a user owns, serially, inside the request. Same defect, worse. It needs orchestration rather than a fire-and-forget invoke, because it reports per-project counts and deletes the user record after the projects. Open in tracker bucket 14.

Defect 2 from the same recon: a project large enough to push its video job
over DynamoDB's 400KB item limit cannot render at all. Researched and designed

The ceiling is measured rather than guessed. Across 83 prod VIDEO_CONTENT#

dispatched 323 and failed eight times. The scaling variable is photos and
clips, not top-level videoItems entries, because a memory can wrap many

it is not.

payloads 5.2 to 7.6x, which clears 1,000 items. But MAX_UPLOADS_PER_PROJECT
deliberately does not count derived clips, and limits.js puts those at about
20% of items, so a project legitimately at the cap holds roughly 1,200 rows.
gzip lands at 76 to 83% of the budget there, with no room for one new
per-item field and none to raise the cap. It moves the ceiling; S3 removes it.

The delete cascade is the real risk and it has three paths, not one. Research
also turned up a pre-existing leak: deleteVideoHandler removes both DynamoDB
rows and never deletes the rendered mp4, though s3Key is in scope. Fixing that
is in scope for the implementation.

DeleteObject but not PutObject. The renderer needs nothing, because its role
carries AmazonS3FullAccess, which is itself worth a look in bucket 4 along
with an inline policy that names dev buckets while running on prod.

5 picks up the one deferred item: what the maximum supported project size

body:
Follow-up to #208. Workflow and docs only, no code.

## The problem

The renderer *reads* what the backend *writes*, so the reader has to be upgraded first. `deploy-prod.yml` had it backwards:

```yaml
deploy-processing:
  needs: deploy-backend
```

A tag shipped the backend and the renderer caught up several minutes later. Every render started in that gap fails.

Two changes have already had that shape: the 2026-08-03 SQS pointer, and the 2026-09-14 move of the render payload to S3 (#208). Both had to be released by deploying the prod renderer by hand ahead of the tag. An instruction written in two docs that the pipeline actively works against is not a safeguard.

## The change

`deploy-processing` now hangs off `validate`, and `deploy-backend` waits for it. Deploying a newer renderer on its own is always safe, because it handles every older payload shape, so nothing is given up by putting it first.

| Job | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `deploy-processing` | `needs: deploy-backend` | `needs: validate` |
| `deploy-backend` | `needs: validate` | `needs: [validate, deploy-processing]` + guard |
| `deploy-frontend` | `needs: deploy-backend` | unchanged |
| `deploy-cloud-run` | `needs: validate` | unchanged |

## The guard is load-bearing, please don't simplify it

```yaml
if: |
  always() &&
  needs.validate.result == 'success' &&
  (needs.deploy-processing.result == 'success' || needs.deploy-processing.result == 'skipped')
```

`deploy-processing` is **skipped** on a manual dispatch unless `skip_processing` is explicitly false, and GitHub skips the dependents of a skipped job. Reduced to a plain `needs: deploy-processing`, a manual dispatch with default inputs would deploy **nothing** while still reporting success. Treating `skipped` as a pass is what prevents that.

Every trigger path, walked:

| Trigger | `deploy-processing` | `deploy-backend` | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tag push | runs | runs after it | renderer first ✅ |
| Tag push, renderer deploy fails | failure | **skipped** | backend blocked — new, and intended |
| Dispatch, `skip_processing` default (true) | skipped | **runs** | backend + frontend only, same as today ✅ |
| Dispatch, `skip_processing` false | runs | runs after it | ✅ |
| Dispatch without `confirm: deploy` | skipped | skipped | nothing deploys ✅ |

## Two deliberate consequences

- **Releases get slower.** Backend and frontend now wait on the slowest job. The renderer deploy does a pip install, pytest, an instance start from stopped, an scp and a Playwright download.
- **A failed renderer deploy now blocks the backend** instead of landing after it. That is the safer failure: a backend shipped alone is the thing that breaks renders.

## What this does not fix

**Dev merges still race.** `deploy-backend.yml` and `deploy-processing.yml` are separate workflows fired by path filters on a merge to main, so they run in parallel with no ordering between them. A merge carrying a backend-first-incompatible change can still break dev renders for the length of the renderer deploy. Fixing it means merging the two workflows or chaining them with `workflow_run`, which is its own change. Recorded under known CI gaps in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`.

**`deploy-cloud-run` is unordered too.** It hangs off `validate` and runs in parallel with everything, and Cloud Run is also a reader of what the backend sends it. Nothing currently in flight depends on that ordering, and changing two orderings at once in a release pipeline is more risk than it is worth, so I left it. Worth a look if a change ever alters the `/analyze-video` payload.

## Checks

No application code changed, so the behaviour to verify is the workflow graph itself, which is walked in the table above. Docs updated: `DEPLOYMENT.md` (known-gaps entry rewritten from "wrong order, deploy by hand" to closed, plus the workflow table's order column), `VIDEO_RENDERING.md`, `INDEX.md`, `progress.md`, and the S3 payload plan's deploy note.

body:
Fixes the cover photo being invisible on a phone. Frontend only.

## What was wrong

The project you were looking at **did** have a cover photo. `titleCoverPhotoId` was set, the photo was in the timeline with valid storage paths, and the video used it. The phone simply could not show it.

`GenerateVideoModal` gates its entire Cover Photo block on one prop:

```jsx
{timelinePhotos && timelinePhotos.length > 0 && (
```

`TimelineV2` (desktop) passes it. `MobileTimelineView` passed only `coverPhotoUrl` and stopped. So on a phone the whole section was never rendered: no preview, no Change button, and not even an empty state explaining the absence. Four more props the picker needs were also missing: `coverPhotoId`, `libraryCoverPhotos`, `timelineSections`, `onCoverPhotoChange`.

**Not a regression from the S3 payload release.** These files were untouched by v0.1.22; the mobile file was last changed Sep 13.

## A second bug found while fixing it

Mobile had its own hand-rolled copy of the cover resolution rather than calling `utils/coverPhoto`. The copy disagreed with the renderer:

| | Fallback when no cover is set |
|---|---|
| Mobile's copy | **first** photo in the timeline |
| Renderer, and `resolveCoverPhoto` | **last** photo in the **last** section |

So with no cover set, the phone previewed a photo the finished video would not use. The copy is deleted and mobile now calls the shared helper, which carries that fallback itself.

## Testing

`MobileTimelineView.coverPhoto.test.tsx` asserts at the prop boundary, because the boundary is where the defect was — every one of these props was simply absent, which is invisible to a rendering test since the modal's sections are conditional rather than required.

**Four of the five assertions fail against the old code**, including the fallback one:

```
× passes timelinePhotos, without which the modal hides the whole section
× passes the four props the picker itself needs
✓ resolves the explicit cover, including one chosen from the library
× falls back the way the RENDERER does, not to the first photo
× marks a chosen cover as manual so a timeline rerun keeps it
```

Full gate: lint clean at zero warnings, `tsc --noEmit` clean, 1,454 tests, build clean.

## ⚠️ Not verified visually

I could not reproduce the original symptom in a browser. Chrome would not give me a viewport under the 767px `useIsMobile` breakpoint — `resize_window` reported success but the page kept rendering at 1530px — so the mobile branch never rendered locally. The fix and the tests come from reading both call sites.

**So the Cover Photo section appearing correctly on a real phone is unconfirmed.** Worth a look on your device after this lands on dev.

## Doc note worth keeping

`docs/FRONTEND.md` gains a section on the underlying cause: desktop and mobile are two separate implementations that render the same modal, and mobile is the thinner one. It has now drifted twice. The practical rule recorded there is to grep for **both** call sites when adding a prop to `GenerateVideoModal`, because a missing prop is silent — the failure mode is a section quietly not existing rather than an error.

The Create button in "Choose Video Length" was cut off by the bottom nav on a phone and could not be scrolled into view. Frontend only.

## Three things were wrong, not one

| | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Overlay | `fixed inset-0` — laid out against the whole viewport, lower edge under the nav | `bottom: var(--bottom-nav-h)` on mobile |
| Panel cap | `max-h-[90vh]` — `vh` is the full viewport, knows nothing about the nav or iOS Safari's collapsing URL bar | `calc(var(--app-height) - 1rem - var(--bottom-nav-h))` |
| Scroll box | `p-6 overflow-y-auto` with no `flex-1 min-h-0` — sized to content and grew past the panel instead of scrolling inside it | `flex-1 min-h-0` |

All three now match what `GenerateVideoModal` and `ThemeBrowser` already do, which is the behaviour you asked for.

`min-h-0` is the easy one to miss: a flex item defaults to `min-height: auto` and refuses to shrink below its content, which quietly defeats `overflow-y-auto`.

Measured in Chrome at a 375px viewport: overlay ends at **611** where the nav starts at **610**, panel caps at **595** rather than 600.

## The button is pinned too

It sat at the end of the scroll, so you had to scroll past every option to reach it. It's now `sticky` at the bottom of the scroll area.

`sticky` rather than a real flex footer like `GenerateVideoModal`'s: this button renders in **three** different branches of `CreateTimelineLengthSelection`, so hoisting it into the modal would drag that branching up with it for no visual difference. Same result for the user.

## What measuring caught that reasoning would not

`bottom-0` looked obviously right and was wrong. A sticky offset resolves against the scroll container's **padding box**, and that container is `p-6`, so the bar pinned **24px above** the visible edge with content scrolling through the gap underneath:

```
bottom-0   → probe bottom 579, scroller bottom 603   ✗ 24px gap
-bottom-6  → probe bottom 603, scroller bottom 603   ✓ flush
```

Verified holding position across the full scroll range, with the button entirely inside the visible area. I measured this inside the real modal's real scroll container, not a synthetic page.

## Testing

One added test, and it is honest about what it is: a smoke guard that the classes survive a refactor, **not** a layout proof. jsdom does no layout, so asserting positions there could only confirm the assumption that wrote the classes. The real verification was the Chrome measurement above.

Full gate: lint clean at zero warnings, `tsc --noEmit` clean, 1,455 tests, build clean.

## A correction to the last PR

#210's notes claimed Chrome could not produce a viewport under the 767px breakpoint. **That was wrong.** Screenshots come back at devicePixelRatio 2, and I read 1530x784 as CSS pixels when it was 765. Resizing works fine; `window.innerWidth` is the thing to check, not the screenshot dimensions. `docs/progress.md` is corrected, and `docs/FRONTEND.md` now records it so the next person does not repeat it.

That correction is why this change could be verified properly rather than shipped on reasoning.

---

# Also in here: dev deploys are ordered now, like prod

Rolled in on request. CI and docs only, no application code.

Prod was fixed in #209 to deploy the renderer before the backend. Dev still raced: `deploy-backend.yml` and `deploy-processing.yml` each carried their own `push` trigger, so a merge fired them as two independent runs with nothing sequencing them.

**Worse than a coin flip in practice.** The backend reliably wins, being the faster job:

| Merge | Backend | Renderer |
|---|---|---|
| #208 | 2m09s | 3m29s |
| previous | 2m05s | 3m03s |

So the wrong order was the *normal* outcome, not a rare one.

## How

A new `deploy-dev.yml` owns the trigger and calls the two in order. They are **called, not merged into one file** — their job bodies are long, and copying them would risk a silent transcription error in the one place that is hardest to test. Both keep `workflow_dispatch`, so either surface can still be deployed on its own from the Actions tab.

| Job | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `deploy-dev.yml` | — | owns the push trigger, orchestrates |
| `deploy-processing.yml` | own push trigger | `workflow_call` + `workflow_dispatch` |
| `deploy-backend.yml` | own push trigger | `workflow_call` + `workflow_dispatch`, waits on the renderer |

## Two things that are easy to get wrong

**The `changes` job.** The trigger's path filter only decides whether the workflow runs at all. Without a per-surface check, a backend-only merge would also redeploy the renderer — which means starting a stopped m6i.4xlarge and paying its idle timeout for nothing. It fails **safe in both directions**: with no usable base commit to diff against (first push, force push, rewritten history) it deploys both, because deploying neither would look like a green run that shipped nothing.

**The `deploy-backend` guard.** Same trap as #209. `deploy-processing` is skipped whenever only the backend changed, and GitHub skips the dependents of a skipped job. Written as a plain `needs:`, a backend-only merge would deploy **nothing** while still reporting success.

Every path walked:

| Merge touches | `changes` | processing | backend |
|---|---|---|---|
| `backend/**` only | b=true, p=false | skipped | **runs** (skip tolerated) |
| `processing/**` only | b=false, p=true | runs | skipped |
| both | both true | runs | runs **after** |
| renderer deploy fails | p=true | failure | **blocked** |
| orchestrator file only, or force push | both true | runs | runs after |
| `changes` itself fails | — | skipped | skipped (nothing ships, run is red) |

All four workflow files parse. Frontend 1,455 · backend 1,742 · renderer 250, lint clean on both, build clean.

## One doc correction

`CLAUDE.md` told you a merge fires *four independent workflows*. That is no longer true — it is three, one of which runs two deploys in sequence. Corrected there, since that file is the thing you are told to read before claiming what CI does.

## What is still not ordered

`deploy-frontend.yml` and `deploy-cloud-run.yml` remain independent. Neither has an ordering dependency on the backend today. Cloud Run is arguably in the same class as the renderer, since it also reads a payload the backend sends it, but nothing in flight depends on that and I would rather not change two orderings in one PR.

body:
Follow-up to #211, from a real incident an hour ago. CI and docs only, no application code.

## What happened

Merging #211 produced **two push events for the same commit**, 31 seconds apart. Both Deploy Dev runs started, and both began deploying the renderer **to the same EC2 box at once**.

That job does:

```
rm -rf ~/video-processor/src   →   scp fresh files   →   systemctl restart
```

Two of those interleaving can leave half the code on the box with the service running on it.

I cancelled the duplicate and the box came out intact — 25 `.py` files on the box against 25 in the repo, service active. But only because the surviving run finished its copy **last, by seventeen seconds**. The other way round and the dev renderer would have been broken. That is luck, not a safeguard.

**The exposure was not new.** The separate per-surface workflows that existed before #211 had exactly the same hole. Nothing had happened to hit it.

## The change

| Workflow | Group | Guards |
|---|---|---|
| `deploy-dev.yml` | `deploy-dev` | the whole dev pair, in order |
| `deploy-backend.yml` | `deploy-backend-dev` | the dev CloudFormation stack |
| `deploy-processing.yml` | `deploy-renderer-dev` | the dev EC2 box |
| `deploy-frontend.yml` | `deploy-frontend-dev` | the dev S3 bucket + CloudFront invalidations |
| `deploy-prod.yml` | `deploy-prod` | everything prod |

## Three deliberate choices

**`cancel-in-progress: false` everywhere here, against `true` in `ci.yml`.** Cancelling a CI run discards an answer to a stale question. Cancelling a deploy kills it midway through writing files to a live box — the exact state being guarded against. The second run waits its turn.

**The two called workflows get groups of their own.** `deploy-dev.yml`'s group serialises runs of `deploy-dev`, but it cannot see a run of `deploy-processing.yml` started straight from the Actions tab — a normal thing to do ("just redeploy the renderer") that lands on the same box.

**Those groups must not match the caller's.** A reusable workflow sharing a concurrency group with its caller deadlocks: the caller holds the group while waiting for the child that needs it. Distinct names avoid that.

## Left without a group, on purpose

`deploy-cloud-run.yml` — Cloud Run deploys are atomic revision swaps where the last one simply wins.

`e2e-smoke.yml` — manual dispatch only, so a human is already deciding when it runs.

## A note on scope

You approved this for `deploy-dev.yml`, `deploy-frontend.yml` and `deploy-prod.yml`. I added the two called workflows as well, because leaving them out left a live path to the same failure — a manual renderer dispatch during a Deploy Dev run. Happy to drop those two commits' worth if you would rather keep it to what was agreed; it is two blocks.

## What caused the double push

Still unknown. GitHub's events API is serving stale data and does not show today's pushes, and both runs were `attempt=1` with the same diff base, so they were genuinely two separate events rather than a retry. This change makes the cause not matter, which is a better outcome than diagnosing it.

All seven workflow files parse.

## What was broken

`projectDeletionWorker` shipped in `v0.1.23` this afternoon and **never completed a single delete, on any stage**. It died during module load:

```
Cannot find package 'sharp' imported from /var/task/src/lambdas/projectDeletionWorker.mjs
ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND
```

The chain:

```
lambdas/projectDeletionWorker.js
  -> services/projectDeletion.js
    -> services/rekognitionService.js   (for deleteProjectCollection)
      -> import sharp from 'sharp'      (top level)
```

`sharp` is excluded from the bundle and supplied by `sharp-node-layer`. The worker has no layers. ESM evaluates a top-level import eagerly, so importing one Rekognition delete call dragged in an image library and killed the function before it ran a line. **The cascade never touches sharp.**

Same `deleteProjectCascade` called inline from `admin/usersHandler.js` kept working, because that runs in the API Lambda, which has the layer. Identical code, opposite outcome, decided purely by layer attachment.

## The fix

`sharp` now loads lazily inside `cropToFace`, the only function in that file that uses it. It is already `async` and its only caller already awaits, so no signature and no caller changed. The worker needs no layer at all.

## Why it reached prod, and what now stops it

**The tests could not catch it.** `projectDeletion.test.js` mocks `rekognitionService.js` wholesale, so the import that breaks was never loaded. New `lambdaNativeDeps.test.js` parses `serverless.yml`, walks the static import graph of every Node Lambda, and fails if one without the layer can reach `sharp`. Verified by reverting the fix:

```
✕ no function without the sharp layer statically imports it
    projectDeletionWorker has no sharp-node-layer but reaches 'sharp':
       -> src/services/projectDeletion.js
       -> src/services/rekognitionService.js
       -> sharp
```

Dynamic `import()` is deliberately not counted, so the fix does not read as the bug. It has a positive control so it cannot pass vacuously.

**Nothing alerted.** An async invoke that fails twice disappears with nobody listening, and every existing failure email fires from inside a worker's own `catch`, which a function dying in INIT never reaches. New `asyncWorkerFailure` Lambda is wired as the `onFailure` destination on `projectDeletionWorker` and `youtubeUploadWorker`. It runs **outside** the failing process and emails through the existing `sendFailureNotification` path (new `async-worker` domain).

## A second gap fell out of the fix

Re-driving the two stranded projects cleared 43 rows to 1 and 61 to 1. The survivor was `USER_PREFS#<userId>`, which the cascade never deleted. Same shape as the `EMBEDDING#` gap in PARKING_LOT #42: a row type added after the cascade was written and never wired in.

`deleteUserPrefsByProjectId` is now a cascade step, deleting **all** rows under the prefix rather than one, since a project with contributors holds one per person.

## Blast radius

Scanned all 26,494 prod rows for `status = deleting`: **2 projects, both internal test projects**. Zero on dev. No real user deleted a project in the window, and nothing was lost.

Prod is now 83 live projects, 83 `PROJECT#` partitions, **0 orphans**.

## Verified

- Worker probe on dev returns `{"statusCode":200,"deleted":true}` where it previously died at INIT
- Real cascade on a dev project: 39 rows to 0, 17 photos
- Both stranded prod projects cleared; `deleting` scan returns 0
- `cleanupOrphanedProjectRows.js --delete` reaped 5 orphaned rows across 4 partitions
- Backend: 1753 tests pass, lint clean at zero warnings
- Both stages confirmed live: worker has no layers, `onFailure` destination attached

## Note on deploy state

**Prod is already running the sharp fix and `asyncWorkerFailure`** (deployed manually while fixing). The `USER_PREFS` cascade step is **not** deployed anywhere yet. Merging auto-deploys dev; prod picks it up on the next release tag. The gap until then is cosmetic: one preference row per user left behind, and the existing ones are already reaped.

## Also included

The `customer-emails` skill, capturing how founder-to-user email gets written: short, no recount of the investigation, lead with who you are, say it is still in beta, link deliberately, draft never send. Plus one line in CLAUDE.md pointing at it. Unrelated to the Lambda fix, bundled by request.

## Docs

`progress.md`, `INFRASTRUCTURE.md` (new Lambda row, "deliberately has no layers" on the worker), `OPERATIONS.md` (new runbook 1.7, project stuck in `deleting`), `PARKING_LOT.md` #43 (no sweep re-drives a failed delete) and #44 (resolved).

## What you see

Vertical clips land in the landscape frame as a thin strip. Measured on the delivered prod video for **"Ramnagar trip"** (`51de06ea`), running `cropdetect` every 8 seconds:

| Content box in the 1280x720 frame | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `1280x720` | genuine landscape, correct |
| `~730x720` | square: the PHOTO crop path working |
| **`404x720`** | **uncropped portrait. Exactly 9:16. 32% of the width** |

## Nothing was reverted

`git log -S "clip_height > clip_width"` shows the gate untouched since `5cfb30d`. The crop feature is intact. It has never worked for the most common kind of vertical video.

Phone video is nearly always a **landscape 1920x1080 stream carrying a `rotation=-90` flag**. The player applies the rotation; the raw stream stays landscape. `probe_video` recorded the raw size, so a portrait clip was written down as `1920x1080`, the renderer asked `clip_height > clip_width`, got `1080 > 1920` = no, and skipped the crop. FFmpeg then auto-applied the rotation on decode anyway, and scale-and-pad letterboxed it.

That's why it looked fine in testing: a video whose container really is portrait works. Which mix of videos a project holds decides whether you see the bug. In Ramnagar, **5 of 13 source videos carry `rotation=-90`**.

## One root cause, two broken things

**1. The renderer skipped the crop.** Now `probe_display_dimensions` runs ffprobe on the downloaded clip and swaps width/height on a quarter turn, handling both the modern side-data form and the legacy `rotate` tag. `build_clip_crop_filter` uses that; the payload's `videoWidth`/`videoHeight` are only a fallback.

**This is self-healing.** Nothing reads the stored size any more, so every clip already in the database crops correctly on its next render. No backfill, no re-analysis.

**2. `actionCenterY` was never computed.** `is_vertical` in `gemini_client.py` used the same wrong numbers, so rotated portrait video was never classified vertical and Gemini was never asked for the action centre. Only **18 of a 400-clip prod sample** had a value. `probe_video` is now rotation-aware, so new uploads get a real one.

Part 1 makes the crop happen. Part 2 makes it centre on faces instead of the middle of the frame.

## Verified on the real prod file, through the real filter chain

| | Content box | Width used |
|---|---|---|
| Before | `404x720` | 32% |
| After | `720x720` | **56%** |

Also ran the three real prod source files through the new code: the rotated one reports `(1080, 1920)` and yields `crop=1080:1080:0:420`; both genuine landscape files correctly yield no crop. All three were recorded in prod as `1920x1080`.

Square rather than wider is deliberate, per Dimitri: cropping harder starts throwing away video people want to see.

## The design flaw underneath

There were two clip paths disagreeing about what to trust:

| Path | Decided from | Correct before |
|---|---|---|
| `render_video_clip_segment` | database metadata | **no** |
| `_ClipSlideReader` (clips in memories) | `frame.shape[:2]`, the real frame | yes |

The file is always right. Both paths now believe the file. `_ClipSlideReader` is deliberately unchanged, and **no `transpose` filter was added**: FFmpeg applies the display matrix before user filters, so the frame reaching `crop=` is already upright and rotating again would be wrong.

## Tests

17 new tests in `processing/tests/test_clip_crop.py`: every rotation form (±90, ±270, 180, legacy tag, none), probe failures falling back to the payload, and the gate itself. The crop decision was extracted into `build_clip_crop_filter` so it could be tested at all.

Verified against the pre-fix logic: **5 fail, including `test_the_bug_a_rotated_portrait_clip_now_crops`.** Full renderer suite: 267 pass.

## Deploy surfaces

Two, both of which a tag release covers: **EC2 renderer** (`processing/`) and **Cloud Run** (`services/video-processor/`).

Note prod is also still missing the `USER_PREFS` cascade step from #213, which merged after the last manual prod deploy. One `v0.1.24` after this merges brings prod fully in sync.

## Docs

`VIDEO_RENDERING.md` 2.8, `PIPELINES.md` 1.3, `progress.md`. Each carries the "do not add a transpose" warning.

videoWidth/videoHeight are only a fallback for when the probe cannot answer. This
is self-healing: every clip already in the database crops correctly on its next
render, with no backfill.

probe_video is rotation-aware in services/video-processor/src/media_utils.py, so
is_vertical in gemini_client.py is right and actionCenterY is actually computed
for new uploads. It never was for rotated video: only 18 of a 400-clip prod sample
had a value. The face-aware centring was not being bypassed, it was never being
calculated.

Verified on the real prod file through the real filter chain: content box 404x720
-> 720x720, 32% -> 56% of the frame width. Square rather than wider is deliberate:
cropping harder starts throwing away video people want to see.

_ClipSlideReader (clips inside memories) already decided from frame.shape[:2], the
decoded frame, so it was never affected. That asymmetry, one path trusting the file
and the other the database, was the actual design flaw. Both now trust the file.
Do NOT add a transpose filter: FFmpeg applies the display matrix before user
filters, so the frame reaching crop= is already upright.

17 new tests covering every rotation form, probe failures, and the gate itself.
Verified against the pre-fix logic: 5 fail, including the one named for the bug.

body:
## Why

Twenty-one emails went to real users on Sep 15, in two waves: six replies about render failures and feedback, then fifteen asking beta users how their video came out. All of it was composed and sent by hand in Gmail.

The only record of who got what was one gitignored report file. That file is the sole reason the evening wave knew to skip the six people contacted that morning. It would not have survived a third wave.

## What this adds

A new `OUTREACH#` entity, shaped after `FEEDBACK#`, which is its mirror: feedback is mail they sent us, outreach is mail we sent them. It becomes the sixth consumer of the AdminIndex via `adminPk='OUTREACH'`, and **no index change was needed**, because `adminPk` is a type discriminator designed for exactly this.

Alongside it: an `AdminOutreach` page copied from `AdminFeedback`, a "last contacted" column on `AdminUsers` derived in memory rather than stored on `USER#`, and `backfillOutreach.js`.

## Three deliberate choices in the shape

- **`adminSk` mirrors `sentAt`, not `createdAt`**, unlike every other AdminIndex consumer. The entity is backfilled from mail sent before it existed, so ordering by row-creation time would put the whole backfill at the top of the list and bury anything recent. There is a test pinning this.
- **`gmailThreadId` is stored on every row** even though nothing reads it yet. Today it is a click-through to the thread. Later it is the hook that lets a job read reply state out of Gmail without a reconstruction pass. Cheap to capture at send time, expensive to recover afterwards.
- **`channel`** (`gmail` today, `ses` reserved) exists so the open question of whether sending moves into the app can be answered later without changing any record.

## Deliberately not built

Sending, automatic reply detection, and a replies-waiting badge.

Replies land in the inbox as ordinary mail, so that signal already reaches a human. What genuinely had no home was who-was-contacted and what-was-learned. The lesson driving that scoping is the feedback intake: it was built, it worked, and three submissions still sat unread for 16 days. More UI was never the missing piece.

## The Gmail side

A labelling convention, now written down in `docs/OPERATIONS.md` 4.1. Every outreach thread carries both `Outreach` and `Outreach/<Campaign> <Month> <Year>`.

The parent has to be applied explicitly, because Gmail's `label:Outreach` does not match sublabels, and that search is what stands between the next wave and emailing somebody twice. All 21 existing threads are labelled.

## Already run

The backfill has been run on **both stages**, 21 rows each, verified by querying the index directly. The ledger it reads stays gitignored because it holds 21 real email addresses; the script takes `--ledger=<path>`.

Re-running is safe: each row's id is a hash of its Gmail thread id, so a second run overwrites the same rows rather than duplicating them.

Note for reviewing locally: the "Last contacted" column on AdminUsers will look empty in dev. The outreach rows carry prod Cognito user ids, so the join finds nothing against dev users. It is correct in prod.

## One test fixed rather than written

`usersHandler.test.js` mocks every db module the handler touches, and the new outreach import was not among them. Worth knowing for next time: `jest.clearAllMocks()` wipes implementations in that file, which is why it re-establishes each mock's resolved value in `beforeEach`.

## Checks

All seven pre-push steps pass: backend import check, backend lint (0 warnings), 1766 backend tests, frontend lint (0 warnings), 1455 frontend tests, frontend build, docs.

Docs updated with `Last verified` bumped: `DATA_MODEL.md`, `API.md`, `OPERATIONS.md`, plus a `progress.md` entry.

## What merging this triggers

Per the workflow table in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`: this touches `backend/**` and `frontend/**`, so a merge to main starts **two** workflows, `deploy-dev.yml` (which deploys nothing itself, and calls `deploy-processing.yml` then `deploy-backend.yml`, renderer first) and `deploy-frontend.yml`. `processing/**` is untouched here, so the renderer call should resolve to a skip. No Cloud Run, no prod.

body:
Bucket 16 (organic acquisition), phases 0 to 2. Strangers have been arriving since 2026-08-22 with no marketing behind them, and nothing on the site was readable by a search engine.

## The problem

Every public URL returned the same 2,523-byte shell with **37 characters of visible text**, identical for Googlebot and GPTBot. `/about`, `/how-it-works`, `/privacy`, `/terms` and `/contact` were byte-identical to the homepage. `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml` and `llms.txt` each answered `200 text/html` with that shell, which looks like success and is not.

Full recon: `docs/beta-launch/recon-crawlability-2026-09-16.md`.

## What changed

| | |
|---|---|
| `robots.txt`, `llms.txt` | Static files in `frontend/public/` |
| `sitemap.xml` | Generated at build from `publicRoutes.json` |
| Public routes | Prerendered at build time via Playwright |
| Landing page | **37 chars → ~5,200 chars** of visible text |
| Canonical | Added, per-route after prerender |
| `scripts/checkCrawlability.mjs` | Regression guard, exits non-zero |

The three missing files needed **no CloudFront change**. The SPA fallback only fires when S3 returns an error, so a file that exists is served straight through. They returned the shell because they were not in the bucket.

## Three things reviewers should look at

**Trailing slashes.** Output lands at `dist/about/index.html`, and the S3 website endpoint answers `/about` with a **302** to `/about/`. Measured on dev with a throwaway probe, after confirming dev and prod sit on identical origins (both S3 website endpoints, same 403/404 mappings). Canonical, sitemap, `llms.txt` and all seven internal links use the slash form so nothing a crawler follows takes the redirect.

**`dist/index.html` is also the SPA fallback.** Prerendering it would have made a deep link to `/projects` flash the landing page until React routed away. Each prerendered file carries a small inline guard that empties `#root` when the path does not match. Verified in a browser against dev: `/projects` renders the app, no flash.

**Two workflow fixes were required.** The cache rule gave everything except the root `index.html` a one-year `immutable` cache, which would have frozen the prerendered pages and the three crawler files in visitors' browsers for a year. And `npm ci` installs the Playwright package but not the browser binary, so all three workflows that run `npm run build` now install chromium first. Without that, CI would fail on this very PR.

## Deliberate decisions

- **No hydration.** `createRoot` stays. `ThemeProvider` seeds from `localStorage`, so a dark-mode visitor's first client render can differ from a light prerender, and React 19 treats that as an error. This is a readability change, not a performance one.
- **`/how-it-works/` is prerendered but held out of the sitemap** while it is a placeholder. Crawlable if found, not advertised. Deliberately not `noindex`.
- **Soft 404s left alone.** PARKING_LOT #48 explains why: the only workable fix duplicates the route list into a CloudFront Function where it will drift.

## Verification

Deployed to dev and tested there, not just locally:

```
/about   -> 302 -> /about/     /about/  -> 200
guard vs dev: all checks passed, exit 0
/projects deep link: renders the app, no landing flash
```

Backend import check, backend lint, 1,766 backend tests, frontend lint, 1,455 frontend tests, full build with prerender: all pass.

## Not included

`signupRef` tagged links (the last Phase 2 item), the og-image tagline fix (bucket 13), and Phase 3 content work.

body:
Four related fixes, all downstream of one question: what does a person actually see when someone shares a Kindred Reels video?

## The main one: share previews showed a logo

Sampling four live prod share pages, **three showed the generic site card** instead of anything from the video.

Three separate causes:

| Cause | Detail |
|---|---|
| No cover chosen | The image came only from `titleCoverPhotoId`. Two of four had that *and* `projectCoverPhotoId` null, with nothing on `VIDEO#` or `VIDEO_SHARE#` holding an image. |
| A clip cover resolved to nothing | The only test was `storage_path`, and a clip has none. Its `cdn_thumbnail_url` was a perfectly good public image, discarded. |
| The obvious fix was worse | Stamping the original looked right until measured: **1.7MB to 21.4MB**, against ~445KB for the large thumbnail of the same photo. Unfurlers cap `og:image` near 5MB, so a big original renders *nothing*. |

Order is now large thumbnail → CDN thumbnail (a clip's only image) → small thumbnail → original as last resort.

### Why it's stamped, not resolved per request

Resolving reads the project's whole photo partition, and `ProjectionExpression` does not reduce RCU. The watch page is public and hit by every crawler and link unfurler, so per-request resolution would read a 764-photo partition on every preview. That's the read shape that cost $43 in June. Resolved once at share creation, stored on `VIDEO_SHARE#` as `previewImageUrl`, read once.

The fallback order matches `frontend/src/utils/coverPhoto.ts`, which calls itself the single source of truth for covers, so the preview and the app can't disagree.

### Backfill

`backfillSharePreviewImages.js` covers shares already sent out, which is the point: those are the links real people have already given their families. Dry run by default, idempotent, never overwrites, leaves a project with no usable image unstamped so a later run can pick it up.

Dev: **15 stamped, 9 left alone, 0 failed**; a second run stamped nothing. Prod dry run: **23 would stamp, 1 no image, 0 failed**.

## Also here

**`og:description` used a field nobody fills in.** Zero of 21 shared prod projects have a `videoSubtitle`; all 21 have a story. So every shared video showed the site-wide blurb while the sentence the user wrote went unused. Now falls back to the story, whitespace collapsed, truncated at 200 on a word boundary, since a minority use that field as a brief rather than a caption.

**`signupRef` tagged links.** The capture-and-record chain was already built and works (a dev user carries `watch-end` from July). What was missing was anything producing a tagged link. Six agreed tags in `KNOWN_REFS` and OPERATIONS.md 2.3.2. The list is soft, so `?ref=LinkedIn` and `?ref=linkedin` would silently become two sources; four tests keep the list and the docs in step. The crawlability guard now asserts that the trailing-slash redirect drops the query string, so that trap is recorded rather than remembered.

**`og-image.png` is generated now.** Its tagline was baked into pixels, which is why "fix the og-image tagline" sat open in bucket 13 for two months. Now `scripts/og-image.html` plus a Playwright render using the repo's own Lora and the real logo path. Sizes were set by measuring the original's ink bounds, so the lockup band matches exactly. One wording change: "photos and videos" → "photos and clips". Not part of `npm run build` on purpose.

## Structural note for reviewers

The resolver first lived in a single service that `db/videos.js` imported, which had the db layer calling the service layer and broke two unrelated suites at import time. Split into a pure `previewImage.js` with no `db/` import (all `watchPreview` needs) and a db-touching `sharePreviewImage.js`, with the handler resolving and passing the value into `createVideoShareCode`.

## Verification

Backend deployed to dev and checked there, not just locally:

- Three stamped share pages serve per-video images at 325KB / 361KB / 463KB, HTTP 200
- A share whose project has no photos degrades cleanly to the generic card
- Crawlability guard incl. a share page: all passed, exit 0. Its `og:image` line went from `note: generic site image` to `ok: per-video og:image`

82 suites, 1,801 backend tests, 1,455 frontend tests, both lints clean, build green.

## After merge

Prod needs a release tag, and the backfill should run **after** the prod backend ships, or it's inert.

body:
## Why

The funnel stopped at "video shared". Sharing is a high bar for sentimental content and almost nobody clears it, so it was never a good measure of whether anyone liked what we made them. Nothing recorded whether a reel was played, watched through, downloaded, or watched again.

## How it works

Counters on the two records the funnel snapshot already reads, not a new event log and not a second analytics path.

| Record | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `PROJECT#<id> / VIDEO#<videoId>` | The owner playing, watching through, and downloading their own reel |
| `VIDEO_SHARE#<code>` | Anonymous watch-page viewers, plus repeat plays and their downloads |

Every write is an atomic `ADD`, fire and forget, built like the existing `recordShareView`. Per-event rows were the obvious alternative and the wrong one: they would need an AdminIndex partition that the snapshot reads in full, which is fine for a few hundred probe clicks and wrong for playback.

## Decisions worth reviewing

**"Watched" means the reel, not the credits.** Every reel ends with a credits slide, so measuring against total duration would make 100% mean "sat through the credits". Milestones measure against content duration and completion fires at 90% of it, the way Netflix counts an episode.

**Repeat viewing needs no identifier.** The project ownership gate already proves who the owner is, so `play_count >= 2` is a rewatch. On the public page the browser answers about itself from its own localStorage and sends a boolean. No viewer id is ever created, sent, or stored. It undercounts on a cleared browser or a second device, which is stated wherever the number appears.

**A play session is one opening of the player.** The owner's player autoplays on `canplay`, so `play_count` is named and read as "times they opened it" rather than dressed up as intent.

**Downloads are counted on both surfaces, on separate records.** The owner keeping their own reel and a recipient keeping someone else's are different facts. They are never summed.

## Reporting

Three numbers had full history and read correctly the moment this ran. On dev:

| | Dev | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Put on YouTube | 5 of 19 finished reels (26%) | `youtubeUploadedAt`, on the video record since Feb 2026 |
| Share links opened | 34 across 9 links, 3 more than once | `view_count`, since Jul 2026 |
| Came back to make another | 1 of 2 people who finished one | Project `created_at` + video `completedAt` |

Nothing was counting the YouTube upload, and it is a better signal than minting a share link: it is a deliberate act of putting the reel somewhere permanent.

The watch-through curve sits below them and starts at zero, because capture begins at deploy and cannot be backfilled. The page says exactly that rather than showing zeros that would read as "nobody watches these".

Both the overall and stranger cuts are stored. Snapshots are immutable, so writing only one loses the other for that day permanently, the same lesson the probe-click code learned in August.

Return-to-create is computed over every project owner, not the AdminIndex `USER` partition that backs the user funnel. That partition is forward-only from Jul 20, and scoping the metric to recent signups would have discarded most of the answer while looking like it worked.

A per-video drill-down behind `GET /api/admin/engagement` answers which reel produced a number that looks wrong. It is the only live read on that page, loaded from a button, and deliberately not in the snapshot so trend history keeps its size guard.

## Two bugs found by testing rather than reading

- `markShareWatched` parsed stored JSON inside the same guard as its write, so one corrupted value would wedge the repeat marker permanently in that browser and every later visit would look like a first one.
- The share-path update sent an `ExpressionAttributeValues` key its expression never referenced, which DynamoDB rejects outright. Every public engagement event returned 500. No amount of mocking finds this; it took a real call against dev. There is now a test asserting the expression shape.

## Testing

Backend 1855 passing, frontend 1475, lint clean on both, build green.

Verified against dev in a real browser: first visit recorded `play_count: 1`, a reload and second play recorded `play_count: 2` with `repeat_play_count: 1`, and `view_count` correctly diverged from `play_count`. The admin section and the per-video table were checked with real data, and a seeded curve confirmed the drop-off renders monotonically before being removed.

**One gap:** milestone events were never observed in a live playback, because the video file would not load bytes from S3 in my browser. The logic has 13 unit tests covering seek-back, pause/resume, forward scrubbing and the credits math, and the endpoints accept the events, but the end-to-end path for 25/50/75 is proven by test rather than by observation. Worth watching the first time a real reel is played.

## Notes

- Nothing here can be backfilled. Playback counters start at zero on deploy.
- Snapshots are immutable, so the engagement block appears only on snapshots written after this deploys. Hit Recompute to get the first one; older History rows keep showing the "predates engagement tracking" message, which is correct.
- Docs updated: `API.md` (three routes, plus route counts recounted from 177 to 197, which had drifted), `DATA_MODEL.md`, `progress.md`, `PARKING_LOT.md` #50 closed.

- Repeat viewing needs no identifier. The ownership gate already proves
  who the owner is; on the public page the browser answers about itself
  from localStorage and sends a boolean. No viewer id is ever created.
- A play session is one opening of the player. The owner's player
  autoplays, so play_count is named and read as "times they opened it".
- Downloads are counted on both surfaces, on separate records. The owner
  keeping their own reel and a recipient keeping someone else's are
  different facts and are never summed.

Reporting splits the same way. YouTube uploads (since Feb), share-view
depth (since Jul) and return-to-create (since the first project) had full
history and read correctly on day one; the watch-through curve starts at
zero and the page says so. Both the overall and stranger cuts are stored,
because snapshots are immutable and writing one loses the other forever.
Return-to-create is computed over every project owner rather than the
AdminIndex user partition, which is forward-only from Jul 20 and would
have silently discarded most of the answer.

A per-video drill-down behind GET /api/admin/engagement answers which reel
produced a number that looks wrong. It is the only live read on that page,
loaded from a button, and stays out of the snapshot so trend history keeps
its size guard.

Two bugs found by testing rather than reading: a corrupted localStorage
value wedged the repeat marker permanently, and the share update sent an
ExpressionAttributeValues key its expression never referenced, which
DynamoDB rejects outright. Both have tests.

Nothing here can be backfilled. Playback counters start at zero on deploy.

body:
Follow-up to #219, found while verifying that PR on dev.

## The bug

`last_played_at` is written to the video record correctly and always has been. It was never added to the `ProjectionExpression` in `loadProjectVideoStats` (`backend/src/services/funnelStats.js`) — I added `first_downloaded_at` there and missed its sibling. DynamoDB returns only projected attributes, so the per-video drill-down read `undefined` and reported `null` for every video.

**Blast radius: none visible.** Nothing renders the field, the snapshot never reads it, and no stored data is affected. The attribute is on the records and correct.

## Why it is worth more than a one-line commit

A missing projection entry throws nothing and logs nothing. It looks exactly like the feature not working. This one surfaced only because someone watched a reel on dev and I noticed a `null` sitting beside counters that had obviously just moved.

So the fix is one identifier, and the guard is the point. New `funnelStats.test.js` pins the projection against the lists its readers actually use:

- Counter names are **derived from `config/engagementEvents.js`**, not hardcoded, so a seventh counter added there and not projected fails a test instead of aggregating as zero forever.
- Both engagement timestamps are asserted by name, which is the exact bug.
- The funnel-stage fields and the YouTube pair are asserted too. Dropping any of those would not error either; it would quietly move a project out of a funnel stage.
- One negative assertion: `repeat_play_count` must NOT be projected here, because repeat plays live on `VIDEO_SHARE#`. Projecting it would imply the owner's own rewatches are counted somewhere they are not.

Verified the new test fails with the fix reverted and passes with it.

## Verification on dev

Before, every row reported `lastPlayedAt: null`. After:

```
Alps Road Trip 2026  plays 1  w50 1  watched 1  lastPlayedAt 2026-09-18T02:15:30Z
Outer Banks 2026     plays 1  w50 1  watched 0  lastPlayedAt 2026-09-18T02:17:36Z
Colorado 2023        plays 2  w50 0  watched 0  lastPlayedAt 2026-09-18T02:14:49Z
```

Those three rows are also the end-to-end proof of #219 that was missing when it merged: a full watch firing all four milestones, a 50% watch firing exactly two, and a reel opened twice without playing. Milestone capture is now confirmed against deployed dev code, not just unit tests.

## Also recorded

PARKING_LOT #51, found during the same check: a video whose S3 object is gone fails silently in the player, no error and no message. Dev expires video objects after 30 days, so 101 of 106 `complete` records there point at nothing. **Prod has no such lifecycle rule and no user has lost a reel this way.** Not fixed here, since it is unrelated to this change and worth doing when something touches the player anyway.

## Testing

Backend 1862 passing, frontend 1475, lint clean both, build green.

body:
Two unrelated fixes, both found while verifying #219 on prod.

---

## 1. The Recompute button has never worked on a deployed stage

Pressing **Recompute now** on `/admin/funnel` returns a 500. That mattered today: the engagement section from #219 was showing its "this snapshot predates engagement tracking" fallback, and Recompute is the one button that clears it.

The api Lambda role's `lambda:InvokeFunction` permission is an explicit per-function ARN allowlist. `funnelSnapshot` was never on it. From the prod log:

```
AccessDeniedException: ...-prod-api is not authorized to perform:
lambda:InvokeFunction on resource: ...-prod-funnelSnapshot
because no identity-based policy allows the action
```

I added `POST /api/admin/funnel/recompute` in July 2026 and did not add its target to the list sitting ten lines away in the same file. Broken on **both deployed stages** since.

**Why it hid for two months** (now comments beside the list, because it is easy to repeat):

- **The nightly schedule was never affected.** EventBridge invokes that Lambda directly and does not use this role, so daily snapshots kept arriving on time and the page always had data. Only the manual button failed.
- **Local dev cannot reproduce it.** `recomputeFunnelHandler` detects it is not in Lambda and runs the snapshot in-process, which is the path every local test takes.

Same class of bug as the per-index DynamoDB ARNs, which `INFRASTRUCTURE.md` already warns about in nearly identical words. That warning now exists for the invoke list too.

### The banner that made it hard to diagnose

The error banner on that page used raw Tailwind dark-palette classes (`bg-red-900/30`, `text-red-300`) instead of the theme tokens the rest of the app uses, so in the light theme it rendered pale pink on pale pink. The message said "Failed to trigger funnel recompute" the whole time and was unreadable, which is why this had to be diagnosed from CloudWatch instead of from the screen.

Now `text-danger` on `bg-danger/10` with `role="alert"`, verified by forcing the error state in a browser and looking at it.

---

## 2. A leaky test that was intermittently blocking pushes

Second commit, unrelated to the above. The pre-push hook failed on an unhandled error after teardown in `MemoryModal.test.tsx`. It reproduced on `main` at the same rate, so it predates this work.

`should show uploading state while saving recording` resolved its mock on `setTimeout(100)` and returned immediately without awaiting it. The upload completed after the file's jsdom was torn down, and the failure chain is why it read as an error-path bug:

1. the success path calls `setShowRecorder(false)`
2. that setState needs `window`, which is gone, so it throws `ReferenceError`
3. the handler's own try/catch catches its own ReferenceError
4. the catch calls `setIsRecordingUploading(false)`, which throws again
5. that second throw escapes as an unhandled rejection

The reported stack pointed at the **catch block**, which made it look like an error-handling defect. It is not: the error path was never involved, the trace was just the second throw.

Fixed at the leak. The mock hands back a deferred, the test resolves it explicitly inside `act()`, and nothing is in flight when the test returns. Also removes a real 100ms wait.

**Measured, because a single green run proves nothing on a timing bug:** roughly 1 full-suite run in 3 produced the error before, 10 of 10 clean after.

---

## Deploy note

The IAM change takes effect only on the next backend deploy per stage. Merging gets dev; prod needs the next release tag.

Prod already has a snapshot carrying the engagement block, because I invoked the Lambda directly with the CLI after diagnosing this. The page is populated regardless of this PR. This makes the button work next time.

## Testing

Backend 1862 passing, frontend 1475, lint clean both, build green, and the resulting allowlist confirmed to contain all six functions.

body:
About 30 strangers found kindredreels.com organically from late August 2026, and 23 of them made a timeline. All 23 were evaluated by hand in September, and then the code behind them was read. The evaluation found the pipeline picking the wrong items and too many of them, on the path nearly every new user takes. This branch is the six sessions of work that came out of that, run one phase at a time with a stop and a decision at each one.

50 commits, 158 files. Dev only. **Nothing in production was written at any point**, with one exception noted below.

## What a user would notice

**Their video is built out of better choices.** One curator now runs for every length instead of quick mode having quietly become a different pipeline with no clip budget at all. Merit carries a decimal, so photos stop tying with each other in heaps (46% of all cohort photos had been tied at exactly 8). A weak photo is dropped by a rule in code rather than by advice in a prompt. When several near-identical shots are collapsed into one, the one that survives is now chosen on merit rather than by sorting on the photo id.

**Video clips are treated like photos.** They carry the same three judgements, pass the same gates and the same merit floor, through the same functions rather than copies of them. Sideways video is detected and corrected at import, by asking only "is this upright?" of the image and its three rotations. That replaced a design that asked which way heads point, which fails silently on any picture without people, and folding the question onto a call already being made took per-photo upload cost from $0.00359 to $0.00134.

**Things are in the right order.** The capture time inside every video had never once been read, because ffprobe was asked for a field called `tags` instead of the `format_tags` section. An iPhone's own capture date now beats the one a copy rewrote. A photo with no EXIF can take its date from its filename. One sort key replaced six that disagreed with each other, and an undated item sits beside whatever it was uploaded with instead of at the end of its chapter: across the cohort that moved undated items from 69% of the way through their section to 47%.

**Videos open and end better.** The cover photo is picked as an opening shot rather than a generic best-of biased toward the end of the story, and it leaves the body of the timeline so nobody sees the same picture twice in the first seconds. One model call per run chooses a first item that sets the scene and a last item that feels like an ending, seeing the candidates together, which a per-item score cannot do.

**The timeline is easier to edit.** The X that removes an item is visible without hovering. A whole selection can be removed in one action, across chapters. Removing something says where it went and offers to open the Not Included column. The page finally names the drag OUT of your video, not just the drag in. And a Not Included tile says why the item was left out, for the first time ever: the badge's only renderer was a component nothing mounts, so three sessions had argued about wording no user had read.

**The app stops promising what it cannot deliver.** The length picker said "60-100 photos, 5-10 min" for Standard; one real project picked Standard, was asked for 96 items, and got 48 of them and 4.4 minutes. Every line now says "up to". The selection is unchanged, deliberately: of the 62 photos the curator dropped on that project, it called 39 near-duplicates of photos it kept and 13 not relevant, so filling the count back up would put the duplicates back.

## One thing is built and switched off

When a kept photo and a kept clip show the same moment, the check drops the photo, keeps the clip, and refills the place from the same chapter. It was verified on two projects, four removals, and the rule was right every time: all four were genuinely one moment.

It is off because of the policy on top of it. We choose the clip having seen exactly **one** frame of it, a soft 320px storyboard JPEG. On one project that meant dropping a sharp posed photo of a boy and his grandfather holding up a fish, for a motion-blurred frame of the same second. A clip carries motion and sound, a photo carries composition and sharpness, and the rule can see one of those four things. Against a yield of one or two photos per project on about a third of projects, that was not a trade worth making before anyone had looked properly.

`SAME_MOMENT_ENABLED = false`. The module, its 42 tests and the docs are all here. What would settle it is written down: judge a dozen removals against the actual clips rather than a still against a still, then pick one of the five options none of which has yet been chosen on evidence.

## Four decisions, with their reasoning in the Decision Log

- **Stop tuning how items are ranked and selected.** Three new strategies were judged blind against the current pipeline on five projects, by a person and by a model. Nothing beat it. Selections that measured as *less* repetitive were liked less, because the family is what gets photographed repeatedly and spreading a selection out drops the people the video is about.
- **Change the length promise, not the selection.** See above.
- **Build nothing to check whether the people a video is for are in it.** The current pipeline drew zero such complaints across 36 blind judgement-sides; every one belongs to the old selection or to a strategy that lost. Identity on every project would roughly double what a project costs, and `Privacy.tsx` says nothing about faces or biometrics, so extending it past tributes is a legal decision before an engineering one.
- **A date source is trusted by what it does**, never by which app made it, and only after being checked against camera dates on real files. This one was learned the hard way: the evaluation's claim that WhatsApp writes capture times into filenames was built on without being checked, shipped, and then corrected. Honest recovery was 5%, not the 48% first reported.

## What is still not done

Three things, recorded in bucket 17 in the order to do them.

1. **Judge the opening-and-ending choice, blind, on six projects.** The one phase of that session that never happened, while the feature is live and moving the first and last item of every video.
2. **Decide the same-moment policy**, then turn the check on or take it out.
3. **The repeats pass, never started.** Clips never enter embedding clustering, so five clips of one wave all survive. That drives the 65% clip share and 76% of screen time, and it is bigger than the photo-against-clip case this branch did build.

## Testing

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| Backend | 1,996 | **2,358** |
| Frontend | 1,485 | **1,560** |
| Video processor | 0, and no CI gate | **150** |

Lint clean at zero warnings both sides, backend import check clean, frontend build clean, ruff clean. The video-processor service went from no tests and no CI job to a suite and a gate; its `test_clip_judgements.py` had never run anywhere, including CI, and would have gone red the first time this branch was pushed.

Four things this session were settled in a browser because a test could not settle them: whether the remove X stays readable over a white sky, whether the new length strings wrap, how many requests a 20-item removal actually makes, and at what width the drag hint breaks to two lines. The third found a real defect, fixed here: a 20-item removal was making 120 HTTP requests, 80 of them refetches only the last one needed. It is 44 now, and that was never new with the bulk button, since multi-drag has dispatched one mutation per tile since it shipped.

## Production data

Nothing in prod was written at any point in any session, with one recorded exception: three prod clip records had a misspelled frame filename repaired, with approval, two of which are in a real user's finished video.

## Reading it

`.claude/plans/timeline-quality-workstream-summary.md` summarises all six sessions. Each session also has its own handoff beside it, except the opening-and-ending one, which never wrote one.

Quick mode ran its own combined architect+curator because it has no
architect and no naming pass, so something had to author a title,
subtitle and mood. The two prompts then drifted, and quick lost three
things standard had:

  - No clip target at all. Quick passed targetClips: null, which
    disables BOTH guards in resolveCuratorResult, so a project with a
    budget of 6 clips shipped 78.
  - No theme fan-out. The whole pool went in one call, so nothing
    spread the picks across moments.
  - No singleton misfit filter, skipped on the grounds that "quick's
    curator has the not_relevant guardrail" -- which both curators
    build from the same buildExclusionGuardrailBlock, so the reason
    never distinguished them.

Quick was 15 of the 23 timelines the stranger cohort produced, so the
drifted path is the one nearly every new user gets.

Quick is now "one section, quick's budget" and otherwise identical.
Title and subtitle come from sectionNamingService off a curator-authored
summary, gated by curatorAuthorsNaming (deterministic OR quick), which
also sets includeSummaryMood. quickCuratorStep.js is deleted; nothing
imported it and no test covered it. The user's per-section description
moves into the shared prompt as buildUserGuidanceBlock, wording
unchanged.

This also removes a live bug on a path nobody in the cohort hit: a quick
project with a user-chosen section count skipped skipArchitect but still
routed to the quick curator, so each section self-named in isolation and
the naming pass then overwrote all of them from empty summaries.

Verified on dev, Disney World 2018 - 2 and Outer Banks 2024, both tiers.
Clips landed exactly on target in all four runs (Disney quick kept 14 of
116 candidates against a target of 14); totals within budget; titles,
moods, music and covers all present; no exclusion missing a reason or a
stage.

Bucket 17 "Timeline Quality" added to the beta tracker as a launch gate,
superseding the 2026-08-07 decision not to track curation quality -- its
own revisit condition was "if evidence demands", and the cohort
evaluation is that evidence.

commits.messageBody:
PIPELINES.md has said "never send 150+ images in one call" since June,
with the measurement behind it (0/3 blocked at 150, 3/3 at 300). Only
the thematic stage ever enforced it. The curator had no cap at all.

Measured on the Sept 2026 stranger cohort: quick mode sent up to 483
images in a single curator call, and even after moving quick onto the
theme fan-out the largest single theme was still 287.

Curator: CURATOR_MAX_ITEMS_PER_CALL = 100, matching the thematic stage's
margin. runCuratorStep becomes a wrapper over runCuratorCall. At or
under the cap it makes exactly one call and behaves as before; over it,
the pool splits into contiguous chronological chunks that share the
pool's budget via the same computeThemeBudgets used for themes, run in
parallel, and merge. Three properties keep a chunked call
indistinguishable downstream, each with a test: chunks are contiguous
and merged in order so chronology survives; budgets sum to the target so
chunking cannot inflate a section; and the chunks yield ONE cover
nominee, since a chunk is not a theme and must not add a row to
coverNominees. Chunked calls take the tight allowed range
(buildResponseFormatBlock gains tightRange, defaulting to !!themeContext
so nothing changes today) -- the +2 overshoot is per call, so a loose
range across K chunks would sum to +2K on one budget.

Singleton filter: SINGLETON_FILTER_MAX_CANDIDATES_PER_CALL = 40, lower
for a second reason on top of image count. That stage makes the model
account for every candidate id exactly once, and the bookkeeping
degrades with N. Verifying phase 1 yesterday, 87 candidates in one call
came back with 86 accounted for, so the section failed open and got no
misfit pass at all. Batches now run in parallel against the same
reference winners, and a failed batch costs only its own candidates.

Verified on dev. The 87-candidate call is now 3 calls of 29 and finds 12
misfits where it previously found none. Curator chunking was exercised
end to end by temporarily lowering its cap to 30 and re-running Disney
quick: a 164-item theme split into 6 calls whose budgets summed exactly
to the target (7 photos, 9 clips) and merged to 8 and 9; every curator
call came in under the cap. Cap restored before commit. Outer Banks on
standard is unchanged, every section's clips on target.

commits.messageBody:
computeMeritScore rounded the composite to an integer, which flattened
the curator's ranking onto an 11-point scale that most photos crowd the
top of. Across the 3,698 scored photos in the September stranger cohort,
46% scored exactly 8 and 76% scored 7 or above, so on nearly half the
corpus the curator was choosing between items it had been told were
identical.

Measured on Outer Banks 2024 (dev), 120 scored photos:

  distinct values   10  ->  28
  biggest tie       54 photos (45%) at 9  ->  41 (34%) at 8.5

That 54-photo tie splits into 8.5 (41), 9.0 (7), 8.8 (5), 9.3 (1). Three
quarters of what the curator read as a "9" was really an 8.5.

The decimal is lossless for the usual four dimensions: every mean of four
integers is a multiple of 0.25, so 8.0 / 8.3 / 8.5 / 8.8 stay distinct.
Sub-scores stay whole, as the model reports them. The label forces one
decimal (Merit: 9.0/10) so every label is the same width and two scores
compare digit for digit.

Also made the prompt's merit bands continuous. "7-10 / 4-6 / 0-3" put a
6.5 in no band once the composite gained a decimal; they now read "7.0
and above / 4.0 up to 7.0 / below 4.0", with a test that keeps them
gap-free. The keep-zero sentence around MERIT_KEEP_ZERO_BAR still reads
correctly ("no photo here reaches 4/10") and is unchanged.

The frontend debug panel computes this mean independently rather than
calling computeMeritScore, so it was updated in step; a comment now says
so, since it would silently diverge if MERIT_WEIGHTS ever stopped being
equal.

commits.messageHeadline: Give the curator merit to one decimal place

commits.messageBody:
MERIT_KEEP_ZERO_BAR has existed since June but only as prompt text, and
the sentence it sits in is group-level: "if no photo HERE reaches the
bar, keep none". A 3.0 photo in a group whose best is a 9.0 was never
addressed by it, and the same paragraph explicitly invites the model to
override the score. Three sub-4 photos reached real timelines in the
September stranger cohort, two of them in opening sequences.

New meritFloorStage.js, pure code, per section, after the singleton
filter and before the curator. Two rules keep it from doing harm:

  - A thin section keeps its weak photos. Removal stops the moment the
    remaining pool (photos + clips) would fall below the section's own
    total target, because coming up short is worse than one weak photo.
  - An item with NO merit is never a candidate. That covers photos
    analysed before the feature shipped and, until session B, every
    clip. Absent evidence is not evidence of weakness.

Removals go weakest first, ties broken by id so two runs over one pool
agree. A missing target removes nothing rather than guessing, since
guessing would mean guessing in the direction that throws photos away.

New reason low_merit and stage merit_floor. No existing reason fit:
low_quality is documented as technical faults only, and merit is
explicitly aesthetic, so reusing it would tell a user their photo is
broken when it is not. For the same reason the badge ("Weaker shot") is
styled like "Not Selected" rather than like a defect. The detail is the
upload analysis's own meritReason sentence.

The group-level prompt sentence stays exactly as it is. It is a
different and still useful judgement, and it is what makes an all-weak
group return nothing.

Verified on dev. Outer Banks quick dropped 5 photos (2.8, 2.8, 3.3, 3.5,
3.8) from a 105-item pool against a target of 30, each carrying its own
reason; one of those, the 3.8, rounded to 4 before phase 2 and would
have cleared the bar. Disney is the control: 238-item pool, target 30,
so ample headroom, and zero removals because none of its photos carry
merit data at all.

commits.messageBody:
Neither half of the choice consulted highlightMerit. The model's pick
came from a label carrying only a description and a visual signature,
and the deterministic fallback tiebroke inside a quality bucket on the
lexicographic photo id -- in practice a string sort on a random hex
identifier, since almost every candidate is `good`. That is how a 9.00
lost to an 8.75 and a 7.50 lost to a 6.50 in the September cohort: the
pipeline was picking the survivor of a near-duplicate group at random.

Prompt: each photo label now carries the same Merit line the curator
sees, plus one sentence telling the model to prefer the higher merit
between otherwise-similar photos. The pick is still never overridden in
code. To keep the two image-aware passes from drifting in wording or
precision, the line comes from a new shared buildMeritLabel in
curatorPrompts.js rather than a second copy.

Fallback: pickRepresentative sorts quality bucket, then merit
descending, then id. A photo with no merit ranks -1, so it sorts below a
genuine 0.0 without being conflated with one.

Measured on dev: 9 of 20 multi-photo clusters on Outer Banks 2024 now
resolve to a different representative, every change moving to the higher
merit (8.5 -> 9.0, 8.0 -> 8.5, 8.3 -> 8.5, 8.0 -> 9.0). Two of those
four were impossible before phase 2, since 8.0/8.5 and 8.0/8.3 both read
as "8" under the integer score. Disney World 2018 - 2, whose photos
predate the merit feature, changes 0 of 45 clusters, so the id fallback
still governs unscored pools.

Note on the 45%: pickRepresentative only runs when the model picked
nothing or the call failed, so that figure is how often the deterministic
fallback would now choose differently, not how often a shipped timeline
changes. The prompt change is the larger lever and is not measurable
without a controlled comparison.
