commits.messageBody:
Three changes to how a section's budget is decided and recorded.

1. Clamp the target to the pool. computeBoundedProportionalTargets
divides a budget across sections and never compares a target to the
section's own pool; worse, its spread clamp pulls a SMALL section's
target UP toward its neighbours, so a 2-item section can be asked for
11. 19 of 51 cohort sections were asked for at least as many items as
they held. Each section's total is now capped at the items that actually
reach its curator, before the photo/clip split. The shortfall is
deliberately NOT redistributed -- keep it simple, revisit if videos come
out noticeably short -- it is logged, and the clamped numbers are what
SECTION# stores, so the diagnostic matches what the curator was asked.

2. No empty section while the pool holds usable items. New
sectionTopUp.js: after the theme fan-out aggregates, a section under
min(MIN_PER_SECTION, clamped target) is refilled from its own pool,
highest merit first (unscored last), skipping anything whose similarTo
points at an item already in the section, then re-sorted
chronologically. Topped-up items lose their exclusion record.

This overrides resolveCuratorResult's respect for an intentional empty
selection at the SECTION level only. Per-theme calls may still return
nothing -- that is the merit floor working, and the guard there is
unchanged. It cannot hold for a whole section because the renderer skips
an empty section, so the chapter simply vanishes: 6 of 51 cohort
sections came back with zero or under a third of target from a pool of
5+, two of them chapters the user had titled themselves. The pool it
draws from is post quality-gate, content-value, singleton-filter and
merit-floor, so nothing those stages rejected can come back.

The watch-item comment this closes is in curatorResult.js, not
constants.js as the spec had it.

3. Persist the tier. config.videoLength lived only on the organize
draft, which apply deletes, so no project recorded which length mode
produced its timeline and the September evaluation had to infer it from
section counts. Apply now writes lastTimelineVideoLength onto PROJECT#,
named to match lastTimelineStageCounts and written in the same step.
Forward-only, no backfill: null means a pre-2026-09-18 timeline or none.

Verified on dev with 8 forced sections on Outer Banks at comprehensive,
which is exactly the small-section shape these guards exist for. Five of
eight were clamped (worst: target 17 against a pool of 6), one was
topped up (kept 4, filled to 5), and the result had zero sections whose
stored target exceeds its pool and zero empty sections. A section that
kept only 1 photo but 7 clips was correctly left alone: the floor counts
items, not photos. Applying that draft confirmed
lastTimelineVideoLength went from null to "comprehensive", and replaced
the Outer Banks dev timeline in the process.

commits.messageBody:
Removing an item from the timeline clears PHOTO#.sectionId
(memoryHandler.js:1098-1099). Any analysis that reconstructs "what the
pipeline picked" as "items that have a sectionId" therefore subtracts
every user removal before it starts, and reads removals as zero. That is
exactly how the September curation evaluation concluded "not one user
removed an item the pipeline had selected" when the real figure was 32.

DATA_MODEL.md now records both the trap and the rule: a user removal is
ai_metadata.userRemovedFromSectionId set AND no pipeline rejection
(rejectionReason and rejectionStage both null). Both halves are load
bearing. Recomputing from the cohort manifests, 41 items carry the flag
and 9 of those were also rejected by a pipeline stage on a later
rebuild, which makes them ambiguous rather than user removals. The
remaining 32 match the recon exactly: Anniv Papa 14, Rosh Hashanah 12,
Canada & Chicago 6, against 390 additions.

The evaluation report (untracked, reports/) had already been corrected
for the headline claim, the scorecard and both open questions. Two
stragglers fixed there: open question 3 still said "none removed any",
and the cover-nominee table still listed Anniv Papa's 99-scoring image
as "not in the timeline at all" and counted it as a curation failure.
Checked against the record: that photo has the user-removal flag and no
pipeline rejection, so the curator kept it and the user removed it. The
row stays in the table since its point is that a 99-scoring image is not
opening the video, which remains true.

commits.messageBody:
Phase 0 of session B was read-only and found three things worth writing down before
any code moves.

Parking lot item 34, "services/video-processor has zero tests", is REOPENED. It was
closed Won't Do on Sep 12 with its own condition: reopen if the service starts changing
regularly, or if a clip-analysis regression reaches a user. Both fired. The service has
changed four times since (the OOM caps, the global Vertex endpoint, display dimensions,
and session B is about to change it twice more), and the rotated-portrait clip that
never got an actionCenterY is exactly a clip-analysis regression that reached users: one
finished video has 78 of 102 items playing sideways. The closure's other ground has
weakened too, since the F3 smoke test only asserts that the dispatch to Cloud Run does
not fail and says nothing about what comes back.

New item 52: no test anywhere feeds real media to the pipeline. All 243 renderer test
functions assert on strings and numbers derived from a mocked ffprobe, there is no media
fixture in the repo, and processing/tests/conftest.py replaces cv2 and PIL with MagicMock
before the video package imports them. So the whole class of defect where the code runs
fine and the pixels are wrong is invisible to the suite, which is the class bucket 17 was
filed against. Slide rendering is the one surface with real pixel verification.

Two decisions recorded. First, `functional` is retired as an exclusion reason in favour
of `not_relevant`, which the curator's own instructions already defined as covering
functional captures with the same list of examples; users were seeing two different words
for one judgement depending on which stage caught the photo. Second, the exclusion badge
is widened: measured in Chrome at the real font and size, the 60px cap fits about eight
characters, so "Not Selected", "Redundant" and session A's "Weaker shot" have all been

commits.messageBody:
Cherry-picked from db4cfd8, written 2026-09-13 on the local-only branch
dimitri/cloud-run-ci-gate and never pushed. Session B needs a suite under
services/video-processor/ before it changes frame extraction, adds an orientation
call and extends the clip-analysis prompt, so it is landing here.

services/video-processor/ was tested by nothing, anywhere. ci.yml has jobs for
backend, frontend and processing and never mentioned it, and deploy-cloud-run.yml
built and pushed an image with no lint and no tests. Every other deploy workflow
runs the relevant suite first. That one did not, and neither did the pre-merge gate.

There were no tests to run either: the directory was a Dockerfile, a requirements.txt
and src/. So media_utils.py claiming "the parity case table is duplicated in both test
suites" was false, and frameNames.test.js said as much: "That service has no test suite
of its own, so this file is the only executable statement of the padding rule." The
authoritative side, the one that uploads the frames, was the unguarded one. That is the
function behind frame_4s.jpg versus frame_04s.jpg.

38 tests. The frame_stem parity table is the same table the backend holds. The rest
cover needs_transcode and the env-var contract config.py refuses to start without,
including that an empty string counts as missing, which is what --set-env-vars=VAR=
produces. Ruff over src/ and tests/, same ruleset processing/ uses.

The deploy job carried `if: always() && !cancelled()`, so adding `test` to its needs
would have done nothing: always() ignores the result of every need and a failing test
job would still have deployed. It now reads `!cancelled() && needs.test.result ==
'success'`, which keeps the workflow_dispatch path working and makes the gate real.

Verified here before committing: ruff clean, 38 tests pass on python 3.11, and the
backend's frameNames suite still passes at 28.

Four documentation conflicts resolved by hand rather than taken wholesale, because
main has moved 56 commits since this was written. DEPLOYMENT.md and INDEX.md keep
main's newer Last verified lines with today's entry prepended; progress.md takes the
entry at the top dated Sep 18, saying plainly that the work was written on the 13th
and sat unmerged; and parking lot item 34, which the previous commit reopened, is
closed Fixed with both halves of its history kept.

commits.messageHeadline: Test the Cloud Run service, and gate its deploy on that

commits.messageBody:
A video filmed sideways whose file declares no rotation was invisible end to end.
ffmpeg applies the rotation a file DECLARES, so the metadata case has always worked;
the case with no metadata reached clip analysis sideways, read as landscape so no
actionCenterY was requested, and rendered sideways. One user's finished video has 78
of 102 items playing sideways.

orientation.py checks before any frame is extracted, and on a correction forces a
transcode with the rotation in the pixels. Thumbnails, storyboard frames and clip
analysis then read the transcode. The renderer needed no change: it follows the clip
record's gcsUri, which apply points at the transcode, and re-probes the file anyway.

THE QUESTION CHANGED, AND THAT IS THE SUBSTANCE OF THIS COMMIT

It started as a copy of the photo path's head-direction observable, which validated at
94% in June on photos OF PEOPLE. Measuring it anywhere else killed it:

- Its premise fails silently. Asked which way heads point in a picture with no heads in
  it, the model names a direction rather than declining. Of 78 photos rotated in dev, 23
  had no face detected, and the ones with no human at all were wrong every time. I opened
  them: a horse walks on a beach upside down, a dog lies on its side.
- Left versus right is a coin flip even with a clear subject. Seven frames of a genuinely
  sideways video split 4 "left" to 3 "right", two corrections 180 degrees apart.
- Four manufactured rotations of one video all returned "270". RotBench (arXiv 2508.13968)
  explains it: models "consistently default to labeling ambiguous rotations as
  counter-clockwise". It puts Gemini-2.5-Pro at 0.50 for 90 degrees and 0.40 for 270 and
  concludes MLLMs cannot identify image rotation.

What every model IS reliable at is recognising upright, 1.00 at 0 degrees in RotBench. So
the question is now "is this image upright?", asked of the frame and of its three
rotations, taking the one that comes back upright. That is RotBench's normalized rotation
voting, which took GPT-4o from 0.19 to 0.86 at 270. Eight test videos covering upright,
90, 180 and 270, with and without people: 8/8, against 4/8 for the head-direction design
on the same files. The corrected outputs were opened and checked by eye.

It short-circuits on the un-rotated frames, the ~98.5% case, so a video costs three cheap
calls and twelve at worst. And it runs on the LITE model: on 16 real photos in all four
orientations, 3.1-flash-lite and 3.5-flash score identically, 16/16 upright and 15/16
rotated. The stronger tier existed for left-versus-right; the new question retires it.

A rotation is applied only when every sampled frame calls it upright and no other rotation
does. Two rotations both reading upright means near rotation-invariant footage — a close-up
of the moon was the real case — and nothing is corrected. Any failed call stands the whole
thing down.

TWO DEFECTS FOUND ON THE WAY

- The shared Gemini client was not thread-safe. Check-then-assign: three threads each built
  a client, the last assignment won, and collecting the losers closed their transports
  mid-request. It broke two of the first three calls. Now locked.
- The transcode would have overwritten every corrected video's date. Re-probing the output
  picks up ffmpeg's own container timestamp, and the callback uses creationTime to overwrite
  exifDate, so every corrected video would have sorted to the end of the timeline. The
  source's value is carried across, pinned by a test.

Forward-only: nothing backfills existing videos. The photo path still uses the old question
and is the next commit; its orientation call has never been cost-tracked and is the larger
half of what analysing a photo costs.

Verified: ruff clean, 66 python tests, 1,964 backend tests, backend lint and import check
clean. The 8/8 run and the eyeball checks were against dev media, no prod data.

commits.messageHeadline: Detect and correct sideways video at import, by asking only whether it is upright

commits.messageBody:
The commit before this changed the video path's question from "which way up is this"
to "is this upright", because the first one cannot be answered reliably and the second
can. This moves the photo path onto it. The interesting part is not the accuracy, it is
that the question now rides on a call we were already making.

build_analysis_prompt gained one field, `upright`. On the ~98.5% of photos that are
already the right way up that field ends the matter and orientation costs nothing at
all. Only a photo that says otherwise pays for three more calls, one per rotation, and
the winner is the correction. get_head_orientation and ORIENTATION_MODEL are deleted.

  Per photo                          before      after
  upload analysis (3.1-flash-lite)   $0.00132    $0.00133
  orientation (3.5-flash, own call)  $0.00227    gone
  escalation, 1.5% x 3 lite calls    --          $0.00001
  total                              $0.00359    $0.00134

There is no longer any routine call on a stronger tier; the architect fallback is the
only gemini-3.5-flash call left in the system. Measured on 16 real photos in all four
orientations, the two tiers score identically on this question: 16/16 upright, 15/16
rotated. The stronger tier existed for left-versus-right, which this question does not
need.

That $0.00227 was never on the dashboard. The orientation call has been untracked since
June and was the LARGER half of what analysing a photo cost, so every project total we
have shown is understated by roughly that. It is tracked now without a second cost
event: the escalation runs on the same model as the analysis, so merge_usage_metadata
adds its tokens to the same counters, needing no new plumbing through the Lambda
response, the worker or trackCost.

VERIFIED: five stored dev photos in all four orientations, twenty combinations, 20/20.
Two of the five read as upright at every angle, which is correct rather than a miss — a
close-up of the moon and an overhead shot into a dishwasher rack have no canonical up,
and the rule refuses to rotate when two rotations both look upright. The other three
include the horse and the dog that the retired design had already stored WRONG in dev,
and the new question reports both as needing 180.

Two things that would otherwise have been quiet bugs. The stored `upright` verdict is
forced to "yes" after a rotation, the same way `orientation` already was, because it
described bytes that no longer exist and anything re-reading it would conclude the
stored photo was sideways. And an absent `upright` field, from an older prompt or a
malformed response, triggers a direct ask rather than being read as "upright" — assuming
is how the horse ended up upside down in the first place.

Forward-only: the 23 photos already rotated wrongly in dev stay as they are.

NOT TESTED, and worth being plain about: imageProcessor.py has no test suite and no CI
job to run one, so this decision logic is pinned only by its twin in the video
processor, which is unit-tested. Parking lot item 52.

Verified: backend lint, import check and 1,964 tests clean; ruff and 66 python tests
clean; frontend lint clean. All measurements against dev media, no prod data.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Crz4FhSbHCtoUPVi2b6zaV
commits.messageHeadline: Ask photos the same question, and stop paying for a separate orientation call

commits.messageBody:
A photo has arrived with three judgements the pipeline acts on since June:
qualityGate, contentRole and highlightMerit. A clip arrived with none of them, so
filterByQualityGate, filterByContentValue and the merit floor all skipped clips in
silence. Across the 23-timeline stranger cohort, 31% of all timeline items were clips
that nothing had ever judged.

The clip-analysis prompt now asks for the same three, with A.1's exact field names,
nested as geminiAnalysis on the candidate. The nesting is the point: it is the shape the
organizer reads a PHOTO's analysis from, so the photo code gets reused on a clip rather
than copied and the two cannot drift apart in how they judge. No extra model call.

CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED

The added prompt text does not change clip yield. Sixteen dev videos, same session,
prompt with the judgements against prompt without: 11 clips either way. Individual
videos differ by one in both directions, which is variance at temperature 0.2.

Validation fails open PER FIELD: invalid or missing is omitted, never defaulted, and the
clip is never rejected over these fields. A defaulted qualityGate is a verdict nobody
reached; a defaulted contentRoleConfidence would start deleting clips, since the
content-value gate drops on the pair. That path fired for real in the run below: one
clip's merit failed to parse, it kept its other three judgements, and it survived.

MEASURED OVER ALL 164 READY DEV VIDEOS: 140 clips, 140 carrying judgements

  Disney       78 clips  72 good / 6 marginal / 0 reject   65 people 13 place
                         merit 3.5-9.5 median 7.5, 1 under the 4.0 bar
  Outer Banks  62 clips  62 good / 0 reject                52 people 8 place 2 detail
                         merit 3.0-9.5 median 8.2, 3 under the 4.0 bar

Zero rejects and zero functional, and that is the expected shape rather than a broken
prompt. Clip analysis has ALREADY picked the single most memorable 5-10 seconds of each
video before anything is judged; every photo is judged as uploaded. So the two gates will
remove almost nothing from clips in phase 3, and the merit floor is the one that will
bite. All six marginal clips are dark or shaky ride footage; all four under the merit bar
are people-free establishing shots, which is what the merit definition says they should
be, since engagement is 0 with no person in frame. Confidence came back high on all 140,
so the gate's confidence distinction is inert for clips. Noted, not tuned.

TWO SMALLER THINGS

Free text is capped at 160 characters, not for tidiness: every clip candidate rides on
the organization draft, one DynamoDB item against a 400 KB cap, and the largest dev
project carries 116 of them on a draft already at 250 KB. That is 31 KB of headroom
rather than 54 KB.

The apply step ENUMERATES fields rather than spreading the candidate, so createPhoto
needed a gemini_analysis parameter for the blob to reach the record at all. A clip has no
upload of its own, so apply is the only write it ever gets. Pinned by a test, because a
dropped parameter there would leave every clip unjudged on the record while still looking
correct in the draft.

Verified: backend lint and 1,966 tests clean; ruff and 97 python tests clean. All runs
against dev media via frames already in GCS, so nothing was re-uploaded and no deploy was
needed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Crz4FhSbHCtoUPVi2b6zaV
commits.messageHeadline: Judge clips the way photos are judged, on the call already being made

commits.messageBody:
Phase 2 gave clips the three judgements. This makes the pipeline act on them.

Clips reach Create Timeline by a different route from photos: they are produced
during the analysis phase rather than uploaded, so they had never passed through
either gate. A blurry clip, a clip carrying another app's watermark and a clip of a
tailgate latch all went straight to the curator to compete for a slot, while the
equivalent photo was removed before curation started.

filterByQualityGate and filterByContentValue now run over the clip candidates too.
They are the SAME functions, not copies: each took an optional id accessor (a photo
has id, a clip has clipId) and nothing else changed. That reuse is only possible
because phase 2 gave clips the photo path's exact field names, and there is now an
explicit test asserting both shapes read the same field, so a rename on either side
fails there rather than in production.

A gated clip is NOT dropped from the candidate array. It stays carrying its reason, so
the excluded-clip accounting still finds it and it appears in Not Included with the
right badge. The tier recommendation and the estimated length are counted after the
gates, so a clip that will never be curated cannot inflate either.

The merit floor considers clips as well, and photos and clips compete in ONE ranking,
so the weakest items in a section go first whatever kind they are. Ranking them
separately would let a 3.0 clip survive while a 3.9 photo was dropped.

MEASURED OVER BOTH DEV PROJECTS, 140 CLIPS

  quality gate          0 excluded
  content-value gate    0 excluded
  merit floor           4 excluded (1 Disney, 3 Outer Banks)

The zeros are the expected shape rather than a lenient prompt: clip analysis has
already picked the best seconds of each video before anything is judged, whereas every
photo is judged as uploaded. The four the floor caught are all people-free establishing
shots, which is what the merit definition implies, since engagement is 0 with nobody in
frame.

ONE NAME FOR ONE JUDGEMENT

The content-value gate wrote `functional` for something the curator's own instructions
already called `not_relevant`, listing the same examples. Which word a user saw depended
on which stage caught the item first. Worse, `functional` was not in the badge's reason
table at all, so it fell through to a title-cased raw code in the red "rejected for
cause" palette: a red badge reading "Functional" on a photo that is perfectly sharp. It
is one code now, and it is styled neutral like "Not Selected" and "Weaker shot". Old
records keep the old string and both the badge and the lightbox map it to the same words.

THE BADGE WAS CLIPPING THREE LABELS AND NOBODY HAD NOTICED

Measured in Chrome at the real font and size, the 60px cap fits about eight characters,
so "Not Selected" (75px), "Redundant" (63px) and September's new "Weaker shot" (72px)
were all being cut to an ellipsis with the full text only on hover. It is 90px now. No
label was shortened to fit a cap that was too small to begin with.

Neither gate had ever had a test. They have 19 now, covering both shapes and asserting
the rules themselves for the first time: only `reject` fails the quality gate, and only
`functional` at high or medium confidence fails the content-value gate.

Noticed and deliberately NOT changed, because it is a copy decision: the merit floor
uses the analysis's own meritReason as the tooltip, and for a low-merit clip that
sentence often reads as praise, so the badge says "Weaker shot" while the tooltip
compliments the clip. Raised rather than decided.

Verified: backend lint, import check and 1,990 tests; frontend lint, 1,485 tests and
build; the gate and merit-floor numbers above come from running the real functions over
the real phase-2 judgements for all 164 ready dev videos.

commits.messageBody:
Outer Banks 2024 reprocessed end to end so every clip carries real judgements (63 of
63) and every photo carries merit (120 of 120), then the organize pipeline run for real
at both tiers. These are the numbers phases 4 and 5 were owed.

PHASE 4 HOLDS

Kept clips outscore the ones left behind, in both tiers: 8.43 against 7.43 at quick,
8.00 against 6.82 at standard. That is the spec's success criterion. The curator is
ranking clips by merit, which is the whole point of giving it the score.

PHASE 5 IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM THAN THE SPEC ASSUMED, SO NOTHING IS BUILT

Standard tier: 45 photos in pool at mean merit 7.31, 61 clips at 7.69; f_raw=0.708 ->
r=0.677; clips end up 65% of the finished timeline and about 76% of its screen time.

Clips are marginally BETTER than photos on merit, so worth does not explain the share.
The cause is a deduplication asymmetry: photos go through embedding clustering and
cluster selection, which cut 120 down to 45, while clips go through nothing equivalent,
because there is no near-duplicate detection for clips anywhere. 69 videos produced 63
clips and nearly all survived. The pool is biased before r is computed, and the
screen-time ratio amplifies it because a clip runs 6.9s against a photo's 4.0s.

The spec suggested deriving the default ratio from items above a merit level rather than
from all items. That would barely move anything: both pools have near-identical merit
distributions, so a merit filter cuts both proportionally. The lever is giving clips the
same near-duplicate treatment photos already get, which is session E's scope. Adjusting
the ratio before that exists is treating a symptom with an arbitrary number.

HANDOFF

.claude/plans/timeline-quality-session-B-handoff.md, force-added because .claude/plans/
is gitignored and session A's handoff was consequently never tracked at all — an
untracked handoff is the thing that goes missing before the next session reads it.
Session A's is added here too.

It carries the orientation redesign and the published research behind it, the phase 4
and 5 measurements, what to expect from the clip gates and why zero rejections is the
correct shape, how to run the pipeline locally against dev without a deploy, and the
fork-safety trap that makes bulk local runs abort ffmpeg children.

commits.messageBody:
Five of the 23 projects in the September cohort shipped byte-identical images
under different ids inside one finished video, and one did it 35 times. Nothing
in the timeline pipeline had ever asked whether two items are the same file, so
every stage treated the copies as two separate photos.

New fileContentHash answers "same bytes?" where deviceFileKey answers "same
name, same byte count?". The second is needed because the first structurally
cannot cross the Google Photos line: all 5,353 prod imports store originalName
as a synthetic google-photos-<id> and throw the real filename away. Items are
grouped by union over both keys, so a record written before hashing and one
written after still meet through name and size. An item with neither is never
grouped with anything.

Videos get their identity for free and photos do not, which is not a choice. A
photo's stored object is rewritten in place during processing, HEIC to JPEG and
sideways to upright, so its checksum afterwards describes the processed image;
the hash is taken in the worker while the original is still in memory, and only
for new uploads. A video's source.mp4 is never overwritten, so the checksum GCS
computed on upload is still readable today, for videos uploaded months ago.

Which copy stays is decided by the user's own work, not by quality, since the
bytes are identical: the manual cover, then a memory, then a caption, then a
corrected date, then the earliest upload, then the id. The surviving id is the
one the cover choice and the memory point at.

Nothing is deleted and no upload is blocked. The copies that are not kept go to
Not Included with a pointer to the one that stayed. The tile reads "Same file"
and the lightbox "Same file, uploaded twice": the tile caps its label at about
twelve characters, and its tooltip carries the detail line anyway. A duplicate
video has no tile of its own, so its clips carry the reason, annotated after the
clip gates so the duplicate reason wins over a quality one.

Verified on Mom & Pop Turn 70 (10 repeated files, 12 extra copies, the earliest
kept every time) and end to end on Outer Banks 2024 with a controlled copy.

commits.messageBody:
Two clips in a real user's finished video carry a URL ending frame_8s.jpg
where the object is frame_08s.jpg. Three records in prod, five in dev.

The producer was still open. The extractor pads every frame name to two
digits, and the 2026-09-11 fix closed the backend's copy of that rule but
left the model's own answer untouched: Gemini's representativeFrame went
into the URL exactly as typed. The answer is now read for its second and
the name re-derived through frame_stem.

That uncovered the same fault from the other side. The fallback used the
clip's midpoint, and a 3-to-8 clip's midpoint is 5, which on a two-second
cadence was never written. Both paths now snap to a frame that actually
exists, preferring one inside the clip.

A dead thumbnail does not cost one picture. Measured against the real API,
a gs:// URI for a missing object returns 404 for the WHOLE request, and
callGemini retries only on 429, so it reaches runCuratorCall's catch and
the section falls open to a chronological take. Every other item in that
call loses its judgement, and it looks like a safety block in the logs.
The curator and the thematic stage now test the URL first: an unpadded
name is provably an object nobody wrote, so the clip goes in described but
not shown, with a warning naming it. String-only by design; a real
existence check would cost a GCS request per clip on every run.

scripts/repairClipFrameUrls.js repairs the records already written this
way. Dry run by default. It rewrites the filename only, leaving the
retired cdn.kindredreels.com host that some of the same records carry,
which is a separate decision.

The naming family moved together into media_utils.py, which also makes it
importable without the Gemini SDK.

commits.messageBody:
Both previous handoffs carried the same open item: nothing caps how many
Gemini calls a timeline run has open at once. Every stage caps its own
fan-out; nothing capped the sum. Building it was straightforward. Measuring
it changed what it should be.

A standard organize of Outer Banks 2024: 34 calls, peak 10 at once, and
that 10 is CLUSTER_SELECTION_CONCURRENCY already batching rather than a
fan-out running free. The curator opens sections x themes x chunks calls,
all three bounded by how the pipeline is built, so even a 1,000-photo
project on the longest tier lands around 40 to 50. There is no path to
thousands short of a defect.

There is also no number from Google to tune to. Read off the live quotas
on gen-lang-client-0328334875: gemini-3.1-flash-lite and gemini-3.5-flash
have NO per-project request quota. Older models do (gemini-1.5-flash
200/min, gemini-1.5-pro 60/min); the current ones run on a shared pool and
slow you down when it is busy rather than at a readable line. The real
protection is the 429 retry that was already there.

So this is a backstop, not a throttle: 100, far above anything a healthy
run does, low enough that a bug firing calls in a loop stops at 100 rather
than ten thousand. Three reasons a real limit might earn its place do not
apply: it saves no money (concurrency changes how fast you spend, not how
much), no memory (Gemini is sent links to images, not images), and it makes
the 15-minute Lambda timeout MORE likely on a big project, not less.

In callGemini rather than at each call site, so a new call site is covered
the day it is written. Same shape as the 150-images-per-call principle,
which was a rule with no enforcement while quick mode sent 483.

Proved it limits something by dropping it to 3 and re-running: peak exactly
3, same 26 photos and 46 clips across the same 4 sections. Wall clock is
not the measurement; four runs ranged 37s to 143s with no relationship to
the ceiling.

A test caught a real hole while being written: Math.max(1, NaN) is NaN and
nothing compares true against NaN, so a non-numeric ceiling would have
silently stopped gating while looking like a gate.

Several people organizing at once are several Lambdas with a count each.
The dial for that is reservedConcurrency on aiProducerWorker, currently
unset. PARKING_LOT 56.

commits.messageBody:
chronoKeyOf builds the sort key for an item. A clip has no date of its
own, so it takes its source video's date and adds how far into the video
it starts. The date is in milliseconds, the offset is in seconds, and this
added them without converting: thirty seconds into a video read as thirty
thousandths of a second. temporalSegmentation.js and thematicStage.js do
the same sum and both convert; this was the one that did not.

It has never produced a visibly wrong order. Every clip of one video
shares a base, and this function has only ever sorted photo ids, so the
clip branch was unreachable in practice. That stops being true the moment
anything sorts photos and clips against each other.

The mistake had a test holding it in place: the existing case asserted
base + 30 for a clip thirty seconds in. Rewritten, plus four more. A clip
thirty seconds in sorts after a photo taken ten seconds in; two clips of
one video stay forty-three seconds apart; a missing offset reads as the
start of the video; and a clip with no datable source returns exactly the
end-of-list value rather than that value plus an offset, which rounds
unpredictably at that size.

commits.messageBody:
Messaging apps strip EXIF on export and write the capture time into the
name instead. Across the 23 timelines real strangers made, 274 of 572
undated photos (48%) were carrying their date in the filename the whole
time, and one project had 109 photos with no EXIF at all, every one of
them named PHOTO-2026-07-20-20-37-24.jpg.

getEffectiveDate now reads the name, between EXIF and the visual
estimate. Derived at read time from original_name, so nothing is stored
and nothing needs backfilling.

Nine patterns; two of the three most common shapes in the cohort were
found by counting real uploads rather than from the plan. The guards are
the substance: an eight-digit run counts only behind a known prefix or
ahead of a six-digit time, every field is range-checked, and the date
must round-trip, so IMG_0045, C00A4494 and bare digit runs return null.

A filename time is a naive wall clock, so it is tagged tzEvidence
'filename' and shifted like a camera clock.

commits.messageHeadline: Read a photo's date out of its own filename

commits.messageBody:
probe_video asked ffprobe for `format=duration,tags`. Container tags are
their own section and the selector is `format_tags`; `format=...,tags`
asks for a field named "tags", which does not exist. So creation_time was
None on every video ever processed, the branch that would have used it
never ran, and zero records in either stage carry tzEvidence
'container-utc' (1,171 dev, 501 prod). Every direct upload was dated by
the browser's file mtime, which for a copied or exported file is the copy
date. That is why ten evaluated projects had photo and video ranges that
could not overlap.

Probing 48 real user uploads, header only: 35 carry a capture time
nothing had read, and 34 of those land on a day the project was taking
photographs.

Two guards go in with it because neither is separable:

- An epoch creation time counts as missing. Google Photos zeroes the
  field on every file it exports, so 16 of 20 dev videos report 1970;
  reading it would stack them at the front of every timeline.
- A Google Photos import keeps its own date. The import writes it and
  then dispatches, so the callback always runs second.

A video's date is now resolved rather than read: corrected, then a real
capture time, then the filename, then a file mtime. A mtime within 24
hours of its upload counts as no date unless the project's own photos
cover that calendar day, by day and not by clock time.

commits.messageBody:
There are two dates inside an iPhone video. `creation_time` is rewritten
every time the file is copied, exported or AirDropped;
`com.apple.quicktime.creationdate` survives from the camera. On all 12
real user files carrying both, the two name different days and the Apple
one is right: an island holiday's eight videos read 26 August from
`creation_time`, inside a 64-second window that is plainly one bulk
export, and 11 to 16 June from the Apple tag.

Reordered, that project's videos go from a block starting at position 24
of 40 to interleaving with the photos from position 8.

The Apple tag also carries the local offset the phone was set to, and
Samsung records the same thing in its own tag beside an already-UTC time.
Both are normalised to +HH:MM and stored in exifTzOffset with
tzEvidence 'exif-offset', which is what that value already means for a
phone photo, so the chronology step needed no change.

Videos can now reveal a project's local zone, where only phone photos
could before. Across all 23 evaluated projects exactly one changes, and
its offset is +00:00, so no photo moves. This is for the next trip shot
on a phone and a camera together.

commits.messageHeadline: Prefer the date an iPhone kept over the one a copy rewrote

commits.messageBody:
Three commits ago this read four messaging-app filename shapes as capture
times and claimed it recovered 48% of the cohort's undated photos. The
claim was wrong and so was the change. The honest figure is about 5%.

It came from the 2026-09-18 evaluation, which said WhatsApp "strips EXIF
and writes the capture time into the name". It does not. A WhatsApp or
Signal filename records when the media ARRIVED on the phone. For a photo
shared the same afternoon those match; for someone dumping years of old
photos into a family chat they do not, and the name cannot tell you which
happened. That claim was built on without being checked.

No WhatsApp-named photo in the cohort has EXIF to compare against, which
is the point of the shape, so the test was how the dates spread:

  semaine arc ad jour 1   109 photos, one day, span 1 MINUTE
  25 Years of Love         93 photos, one day, Sept 2026
  ראש השנה 2026            16 photos, one day, span 173 minutes

The first is the evaluation's own headline example, a ten-stop itinerary
that produced one undifferentiated chapter; a ten-stop day did not happen
in sixty seconds, and those dates would not have let the segmenter cut it
either. The second is a silver wedding anniversary whose EXIF-dated
photos run 2014 to 2023, so this was about to build it a phantom final
chapter out of a save operation.

Removed: WhatsApp iOS, WhatsApp desktop, WhatsApp Android, and Signal,
which names files the same way and had no cohort examples to argue from.
Cohort recovery drops from 274 undated photos to 28.

What remains was each checked against real EXIF on files carrying both:
bare YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS 198/198, dashed date plus time 136/136,
Android/Pixel 17/17, DJI 10/10.

The evaluation report and its recon are corrected in place. The weaker
use of these names, ordering undated items without dating them, is
parking lot 57.

Six steps put a section in order. segmentByTime, the thematic fallback
and the section top-up read effectiveDate then exif_date. Audio-zone
grouping read the RAW exif_date alone, so it never saw a resolved date
and never added a clip's start offset. The two apply sites read the
stored exifDate. Every improvement to date resolution therefore landed in
some steps and was discarded by the others, and a section's order
depended on which steps happened to run.

All six now call buildSortKeys (sortTime.js). A key is the item's own
resolved date; for a clip, its source video's plus startTime in seconds
onto a date in milliseconds; and for an item with no date, the date of
the nearest dated item in UPLOAD order, plus a millisecond per position.

An undated item used to sort to Infinity and land at the end of its
chapter. Rebuilding the cohort's orders both ways: undated items move
from a mean 69% to 47% of the way through their section, and from 20.4 to
6.4 positions from the item they were uploaded beside. KK's Bat Mitzvah
stops closing on six undated photos in a row.

orderedItems is now written on every section with clips, so apply has one
authority. A photo-only themed section is still not re-sorted after the
curator, deliberately: it is grouped by theme.

Audio-zone grouping had no tests; it has nine now.

Two days ago filenames were read as capture times on the strength of a
sentence in a report. The fix that day removed four messaging-app shapes
by name, which left a list of which app writes which kind of filename to
maintain forever. That list can also never be checked where it counts:
the only way to learn an app's naming semantics is to compare against
EXIF, and the files this exists for have none. WhatsApp had zero
checkable files in the whole cohort.

So filenameDate.js no longer knows what an app is. Two patterns ask only
whether a name holds an unambiguous date AND time, covering every shape
the seven app-specific ones covered across 4,167 real filenames. A time
is required, so an eight-digit counter cannot pass.

A date's source is now strong or weak. Strong means checked against
camera dates on real files: the user's correction, a photo's EXIF, a
video container, a Google import. Weak means it might be a capture time
and might be an arrival time: the filename, and a file mtime.

weakDateGuard.js judges each weak source per PROJECT, never per item,
because one timestamp says nothing and a hundred inside a minute says
everything. Either behaviour condemns the group: bunching like a bulk
save (3+ in one minute and over 30% of the set, the same test and number
checkExifSanity already uses, which fits unchanged), or sitting within a
day of its own upload on a day the project's strong-dated photos do not
cover. The video-only 24-hour rule is now this one shared rule.

Proven on the cohort with the messaging shapes parsed again: 3 of 3
chat-export clusters caught, 0 of 51 camera-written filename dates
wrongly dropped.

commits.messageBody:
effectiveDate was worked out during a Create Timeline run and thrown away
with it. So the app showed a simpler guess, from FIVE private copies of
the rule in SortStage, chronologicalInsert, lightboxUtils (twice),
TimelineV2 and TimelineV2RightPane. None of them knew about a filename
date, the check that distrusts EXIF on a scanned photo, a video's
container time, or the guard that throws out a project's weak dates when
they are a bulk save. A photo could display as undated and then be
ordered as though it had a date.

Every API photo shape now carries effectiveDate + effectiveDateSource,
from the new shared/projectDates.js. The frontend reads it through one
helper, utils/photoDate.ts, and works nothing out itself.

Resolved per PROJECT, not per item: a weak date is only judged against
its project's other dates from the same source, and a clip reads its
source video. The single-photo routes therefore load the project. That
is one extra query, deliberately, because the alternative is the same
photo reporting one date from the list endpoint and another from the
detail endpoint.

effectiveDate: null is an ANSWER, not a gap. The backend looked and will
not vouch for what it found, so the helper returns null rather than
falling back to the date the guard just rejected.

Verified in the running dev app on two real items. A bulk-copied video's
clip comes back undated and lands at the end when added. A photo named
PXL_20240217_195356956.MP.jpg, with no EXIF at all, comes back dated
February 2024 from its name and lands first in a 2025-2026 chapter.

Also filed parking lot 58: thematicStage reads aiMetadata where records
carry ai_metadata, so its cluster expansion has never run for photos.
Every section in a real run shows reps equal to items.

first thing a viewer sees and rules out a setup shot. A tribute names the

photo" become one function: best photo of people by merit, then best by merit,
then the first photo. Those copies read a field the database layer does not

backend/src/utils/coverPhoto.js is deleted.

in September; photos go out through the same mechanism and had none. All
five senders now check first and fail open per photo: the curator, the
singleton filter, cluster selection, theme grouping and the visual-signature
backfill.

checked carry a well-formed address, and analysis already sets aside a photo
with no gcs_uri. It covers the gap between the phases: organize re-reads
every record from DynamoDB after analysis, so a record that lost its address
in between would put an empty value in the request and take the call with it.

commits.messageBody:
The title card shows the cover and plays before anything else. Most videos
have one chapter, so nothing comes between the title slide and the first item,
and a cover left in the body was shown twice inside a few seconds.

by hand does the same thing; the previous cover loses its label and its scores

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: The cover photo leaves the timeline body

commits.messageBody:
A timeline in date order is accurate and not moving. People photograph the
setup before the event, so the first photo taken is the emptiest one, and the
last thing that happened is rarely the right last shot. Across 23 real
timelines, openers worked about half the time and closers failed 16 times in
23; one person asked for a specific closing photo and got it at position 58 of
70, after the pipeline had scored it 97 out of 100.

Once the selection is final, one call asks which photo in the first chapter
sets the scene and which in the last feels like an ending. It sees them
together, which a score for each photo on its own cannot do. Two items move;
nothing else about the selection changes.

It will not move a photo it rated below 6, will not end the video on a photo
with no date, will not pick the cover or anything inside a group, and does
nothing at all if the call fails. If the person's own words asked for a
particular opening or ending, that wins and the rating stops applying.

The move is written to both lists that matter, since a chapter with clips
stores its order one way and a photo-only chapter another. Behind one switch
so it can be judged blind.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: Choose how the video opens and how it ends

commits.messageBody:
What someone types per chapter in the Create Timeline modal reached the part
that decides which photos go in which chapter, and stopped there. The part that
picks the actual photos never saw it, except on a one-chapter video where that
path sets the description itself.

Matching them on is not free. The descriptions arrive as a plain ordered list of
strings with no id and no title, so position is the only handle there is, and
the number of chapters the model returns is enforced by a sentence in the prompt
and nothing else. A separate rule merges a two-chapter answer into one, which
can turn four configured chapters into one.

So: match by position when the architect returned exactly the configured number,
counted after that merge, and otherwise pass nothing and warn with the project
and both counts. A description on the wrong chapter is worse than none, because
the curator then picks photos against the wrong brief. The same list decides
which words the opening and ending choice sees for the first and last chapter.

Also: that choice could be told it had followed the person's instructions on a
project where they had written nothing. The claim skips the score bar, so a weak
photo could have been pinned as though it were asked for. It is now refused
unless words were sent, and the model is no longer invited to claim it when
there are none.

Parking lot 59, 60 and 61 hold the unenforced count, the merge, and the id that
would make the match exact.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: A chapter's own description reaches its own curator

commits.messageBody:
Every clip candidate now gets an embedding at organize time, so a photo and a
clip can be compared against each other at all.

Smaller than the spec assumed. Cloud Run has embedded each clip's representative
frame since 2026-05-21 (processor.py step 8.5) and the callback writes the rows,
so on a current project this reads them and computes nothing. The investigation
reported that nothing writes a clip embedding; it searched for putEmbedding and
the clip path uses batchPutEmbeddings. Outer Banks 2026's 43 rows were written on
the two days its videos were processed, which is the production path. What is
real is the gap for anything older: Disney World 2018 - 2 had 115 clips and zero
rows because its videos went through in March 2026.

Also fixed: a clip candidate carries representativeFrameUrl and a clip record
carries cdn_thumbnail_url. clipUrlToGcsUri read only the second, so every clip
candidate was unembeddable.

The three-tier lookup (stored row, legacy inline, compute and write back) is now
one function shared by the photo and clip passes instead of a second copy.

Fail-open: an unusable frame address is skipped before anything is spent, a clip
that cannot be fetched or embedded has no vector, and nothing throws. Not behind
GEMINI_MAX_IN_FLIGHT; that gate counts Gemini calls and these go elsewhere.

Verified on Disney World 2018 - 2 in dev: 115 rows written, $0.0230, and a second
pass computed nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: Old videos get their clips measured too

commits.messageBody:
When a kept photo and a kept clip show the same moment, the clip stays and the
photo leaves, with its place refilled from the same chapter. Built, tested,
verified by eye, and SWITCHED OFF (SAME_MOMENT_ENABLED = false).

Nothing compared a photo with a clip before. Photos go through embedding
clustering, clips go through nothing equivalent, and the two budgets are filled
independently, so a family swim could ship as a still and as six seconds of video
a few seconds apart.

The rule needs two things together: the photo's time inside the clip's window or
within 120s of either end, AND the pair ranking in the top 0.5% of that project's
own photo-to-clip similarities. Never an absolute cosine (the value at that rank
is 0.80 on one dev project and 0.68 on another) and never ranked against
photo-to-photo similarities (a clip's frame is a soft 320px image). Silent below
500 comparisons, which is most projects, because a rank over 130 comparisons is
not a measurement.

Both sides need a date precise enough to mean it: corrected, EXIF or container,
or a guard-passed filename. Never a file copy time, never a visual estimate.

WHY IT IS OFF. Verified on Outer Banks 2024 at standard (3 pairs, 2 removed) and
Disney World 2018 - 2 at quick (21 pairs, 2 removed, 2 refilled). The rule was
right every time: all four are genuinely one moment. The policy on top of it is
what is unresolved. We pick the clip having seen ONE frame of it, so Outer Banks
dropped a sharp posed shot of a boy and his grandfather holding up a fish for a
motion-blurred frame of the same second. A clip carries motion and sound, a photo
carries composition and sharpness, and the rule sees one of those four things.
Against a yield of one or two photos per project on a third of projects, that is
not a trade to make unlooked-at. To revisit: judge a dozen removals against the
actual clips rather than one frame each, then pick a side from the five options
in the investigation's section 2.4.

Two things found while building it:

Membership in a memory is not a sign the user placed a photo. Apply wraps every
timeline item in a one-photo memory, so on a rebuilt project it covers nearly
every photo (70 memories for 70 items on Outer Banks 2024), and protecting on it
blocked a removal that should have gone through. Protection is now a hand-picked
cover, a photo the user captioned or re-dated, and each chapter's cover nominee.

Every pair found and not acted on logs its reason, and a chapter that ends short
logs what it passed over. "3 found, 0 removed" was how the memory bug hid.

Refilling reuses the top-up's candidate ranking rather than a second copy of it,
plus the extra bars: nothing the curator set aside this run, nothing itself paired
with a kept clip, nothing weaker than the weakest photo the chapter still holds.

It said "60-100 photos, 5-10 min" for Standard. Outer Banks 2026 picked
Standard, was asked for 96 items, and delivered 48 at 4.4 minutes.

That is not a defect in the curator. The per-call photo target has been an aim
rather than a quota since June 2026, deliberately, so a thin moment is not forced
to surrender a photo to fill a count. What nobody had written down is the
aggregate: a video about half the promised length. The shortfall scales with
budget over pool size PER CALL, not with the tier, which is why quick rarely
shows it and a themed standard section does.

Every line now reads "up to", and the count names photos and clips together,
which is what the backend budget has meant since May 2026. The two auto-select
messages for projects too small for the picker stop promising counts as well:
"with your 34 best photos" became "from the best of your 34 photos", and "We'll
use all 14 of your photos" became "We'll create a quick highlights video from
your 14 photos", because the gates and the merit floor run however few items
there are.

VIDEO_LENGTH_TARGETS[tier].description carried a THIRD set of minutes and is now
aligned. The picker is authoritative and the backend follows; said so in a
comment and in PIPELINES.md.

Two strings per tier instead of swapping "photos" for "items" at render time,
which would have produced "up to 40 items and clips".

No change to which items are selected. The alternatives are recorded in
PIPELINES.md 2.4 with why each was not chosen: topping up to target would re-add
items at mean merit 4.71 into a selection at 7.14, 39 of which the curator called
duplicates of photos it kept.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: The length picker stops promising a minimum it cannot keep

commits.messageBody:
Each timeline tile has a small X that takes that item out of the video. It was
opacity-0 until the tile was hovered, so the main per-tile way to remove

It now sits at opacity-75 and goes to full on hover and on :focus-visible, with a

Timeline column picks a tile by the video-builder item type, and apply wraps
EVERY timeline item in a one-photo memory, so TimelineV2MemoryTile is what a
built project renders; TimelineV2PhotoThumbnail is legacy items and the right

bg-black/40 at 75% would have left a white X close to invisible over a white sky.

rather than assumed.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: The remove X is visible without hovering

commits.messageBody:
The bar that appears when you select several tiles could only count them and
unpick them. Its own header comment said the pane-specific action was left for
"Session 3" and never landed.

A Timeline selection now has Remove from timeline. It works ACROSS chapters,
which a multi-drag cannot: drag needs one section, a selection does not, and each
selected key carries its own section id. A Not Included selection gets nothing,
because those items are already out and putting one back is a placement decision
a bulk button cannot make. No confirm dialog: every item lands in its section's

photo id the mutation wants needs that section's items, and the provider holds

seconds. There is no bulk route, and one removal cost SIX requests rather than
two: the removal, the persisted flag, and four refetches from
invalidateProjectItemData on settle. The project's whole 341-photo list was
refetched twenty times when only the last mattered. Correct throughout, and it
predates the bulk action, which only made it measurable. Fixed in the commit
that follows; PARKING_LOT 63 carries the numbers.

carrying "You removed" after a full page reload.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: Multi-select can take a whole selection out of the video

commits.messageBody:
Every org mutation ended by invalidating the same four query segments: photos,
memories, stats and video-builder. Right for one edit, wrong for twenty.

Three of them are dispatched N-at-a-time and always have been. A multi-drag out
of the timeline fires one removal per selected tile, a multi-drag between
sections one move per tile, a multi-drag back in one add per tile. Each settled
independently and each refetched everything, so this has been live since
multi-drag shipped. The multi-select Remove only made it measurable.

Measured on a real 20-item removal: 120 requests in 3.5s, 80 of them refetches
only the last one needed, with the project's whole 341-photo list coming down
twenty times.

Fixed with React Query's own idiom. isMutating counts pending mutations matching
a key, and a settling mutation still counts itself, so exactly 1 means "I am the
last one out"; everyone else returns and lets the last one cover them. One shared
key, ['project-item-write', projectId], on all four mutations: shared so a burst
mixing kinds still settles into one refetch, scoped per project so two tabs
cannot cancel each other.

Re-measured: 44 requests, with exactly one refetch of each query. A single edit
is unchanged, invalidating immediately with no timer and nothing deferred.

The 40 remaining requests are two per item and are real work, not waste. The two
ways to shrink them further are recorded in PARKING_LOT 63 and not taken.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: A burst of timeline edits refetches once, not once per edit

commits.messageBody:
The Not Included column is hidden on every load on purpose: that reveal button
is how people discover the timeline is editable at all. The cost was that
removing an item made its tile vanish with nothing to say where it had gone. The
header count dropped by one and nothing else changed.

The toast now reads "Removed. You can find it under Not Included." with one
action, Show, that reveals the column. Several at once read "Removed N items. You
can find them under Not Included."

It OFFERS and never opens. Only the user's click on Show is wired to reveal the
column, because opening it for them takes away the discovery the closed state
exists for. Nothing scrolls to or pins the Removed group either; PARKING_LOT 16
records three failed attempts at pinning.

With the column already showing, the plain confirmation stands: the item is
visibly landing in the Removed group and there is nothing to point at.

One message per action, not per item. A bulk caller removes each item with
{ silent: true } and calls notifyRemoved(n) once, so five removals say one thing
rather than the same thing five times.

The choice lives in useOrgActions.notifyRemoved, fed an optional
notIncluded: { isHidden, reveal } by whichever view mounts it. The legacy Edit
Timeline view passes nothing and keeps the plain string. All four removal routes
already went through one handler, so the X, Delete/Backspace, the lightbox button
and the multi-select action all get it.

The Toast component already had an optional action and an 8s linger for it; the
only plumbing change was widening useOrgActions' own onToast parameter type,
which was narrower than what ProjectLayout passes.

Verified in Chrome across all four cases, including that Show is what opens the
column and lands on the Removed group.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: A removed item says where it went

commits.messageBody:
The Not Included column has always said "← Drag any item to add it to your
video". Nothing said you could drag the other way, so the only route out of the
video a reader could find was a 20px X or a help popover they had to open.

The Timeline column's second line now reads "Drag any item to Not Included to
take it out of your video →" while that column is showing, with the arrow at the
END so each one points outward at the other.

It SWAPS the line rather than stacking a fourth. With Not Included hidden, which
is how every load starts, there is nothing to drag to and the line says what the
Timeline is. With it showing, the reader is editing and the direction is the
useful thing. One line either way keeps both columns three lines tall, which is
most of what makes them read as a pair.

Measured in Chrome across viewport widths: one line down to 1024px, two below
about 950px. The desktop layout starts at 768px, so a wrap is possible in that
narrow band and costs 24px of band height. Wording left alone; shortening it
would lose either "Not Included" or "out of your video".

First tests for this component.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01TuzuxYUWKnQZnNvtGavH2H
commits.messageHeadline: The page says you can drag an item out

commits.messageBody:
No behaviour change.

THE DECISION: nothing is built to check whether the people a video is for are in
it. Three things settled it. The evidence does not convict the current pipeline,

body:
The smoke suite is the eleven-step browser check that runs against a deployed stage: it loads the marketing site signed out, then signs in and walks the critical path, creating a project, uploading a photo and a clip, changing a setting, hitting the tier gate, making a contributor link, and deleting the project. Run [35781100709](https://github.com/kindredreels/kindredreels/actions/runs/35781100709) failed two of the eleven. Neither was a bug in the app: both tests were asserting behaviour that two later changes had replaced, and because the suite is manual-dispatch only, nothing had run it since Sep 14 to notice. Chasing the second one turned up a real gap in the API, which is also fixed here.

## The two stale tests

**About link.** The test wanted the address to end in `/about` and it ends in `/about/`. The trailing slash is deliberate and has been since 41c6241: prerendered pages are written to `<route>/index.html`, and the S3 website endpoint answers the slash-less form with a 302 to the slash form, so the sitemap, canonical tags, `llms.txt` and every internal link use the slash and no crawler takes that hop. The test now pins the slash rather than tolerating either form, so a link that drops it fails here instead of quietly costing a redirect.

**F7 delete.** The test deleted the project, read the photo list once, and expected it empty. It got one of two photos back. Deleting a project stopped being synchronous on Sep 15: the route marks the project `deleting`, answers 202, and `projectDeletionWorker` runs the cascade, because a 450-photo project could not finish inside the 30s request timeout. The dev worker logs for that exact project show the whole cascade taking 470ms and reporting success; the test read the list at about 200ms and caught it mid-sweep. Nothing was orphaned. It now polls instead of reading once.

## The gap behind F7

Three routes take `projectId` from the query string, so `checkProjectOwnership` cannot run on them and they check the project themselves. They checked existence and ownership, not status, so they kept serving a project mid-delete while every project route already 404'd it. The middleware's comment claimed "one check here covers every project route", which was only ever true of the project router.

Two of the three are just inconsistent. `PUT /api/photos/:id` is worse: `updatePhoto` is a DynamoDB UpdateItem, which creates the item when it is absent, so an edit landing after the cascade deleted that photo would write the row back and strand a `PHOTO#` with no project.

The rule is now one function, `isProjectGone` in `db/projects.js`, true both for a project that does not exist and for one whose delete has been accepted. The middleware uses it, and so do `GET /api/photos`, `GET /api/recordings` and `PUT /api/photos/:id`.

`DELETE /api/photos/:id` and `DELETE /api/recordings/:id` stay permissive on purpose and now carry a comment saying why: deleting a photo out of a project being deleted asks for the same thing the cascade is doing, and refusing it would only break the e2e teardown and sweep paths that delete photos through that route first.

**One honest cost.** With the 404 in place, F7 no longer witnesses the cascade finishing, because nothing a browser can see does once the API stops showing the project the moment its delete is accepted. The poll is still right, since `getProjectById` is an eventually consistent read. What covers the cleanup is `__tests__/services/projectDeletion.test.js` and the bucket checks recorded in PARKING_LOT #32 and #39. This is written into the test comment and the changelog rather than left for someone to discover.

## The flaky test

Caught by the pre-push hook, unrelated to the rest. `EditPhotoModal.test.tsx`'s "should show Saving... while saving" stubbed the save with a promise resolving on a 100ms timer, clicked Save, asserted the button text, and ended without waiting. `handleSubmit` then resumed after the test was over and called `onClose()` and `setIsSaving(false)` with nothing left to render into. Vitest reported an unhandled error and a non-zero exit with all 1560 tests passing. It only shows when the timer fires as the suite tears down, so CI has the same coin flip. The test now waits for the saving state to clear, which drains the promise inside the test and also checks that the button stops saying "Saving..." afterwards. Not swept for others of the same shape.

## Checks

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `node --check src/server.js` | pass |
| backend lint (zero-warning) | pass |
| backend tests | 2364 passed, 52 skipped |
| frontend lint (zero-warning) | pass |
| frontend tests | 1560 passed, no errors |
| frontend build | pass, prerenders `/about/` |
| `playwright test --list` | 12 tests compile |

The smoke suite itself has not been run against dev yet; that needs the manual E2E Smoke workflow after this is merged and the backend deploy finishes.

## Docs

`progress.md` entry; PARKING_LOT #68 opened and closed in the same change; `API.md` route notes for both list routes plus its `Last verified` line.

## What merging this deploys

Read from the workflow table in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` rather than memory. This touches `backend/**`, `frontend/**` and `docs/**`, so two workflows fire on merge to main: `deploy-dev.yml`, which detects that only the backend surface changed and so calls `deploy-backend.yml` alone rather than the renderer, and `deploy-frontend.yml`, because `frontend/e2e/**` sits under its `frontend/**` path filter. That second one is a no-op in substance, since the only frontend changes are test files, but it will sync and invalidate. Cloud Run is untouched. **The backend deploy has to finish before an E2E Smoke run means anything**, since the `isProjectGone` fix is backend-side.

body:
Strangers have been using Kindred Reels since August 22. This PR closes the security and privacy exposure that affects them now, found by re-checking every parking lot item against the code and live cloud state. It also replaces the scattered parking lot with one list sorted by risk.

## What changes for people

- **Tribute face matching asks first.** A consent step appears before any face template is made, the backend records it and refuses face indexing without it, and removing everyone from a tribute withdraws it.
- **Privacy policy and terms are true.** They now describe Google Cloud storage, Gemini processing, face templates and how long they are kept, Google Photos, YouTube, Analytics and contributors without accounts. Signup and contributor pages link both.
- **Share links do only what their kind allows (#85).** Group photo links are unchanged. A memory link reaches only its memory, plus the timeline when the sharer allowed it. It can no longer list the library, upload, or record onto unshared drafts.
- **No duplicate or hijacked accounts (#81).** A password signup on a Google account's email is refused. The never-working move-and-disable code is gone. Google joins only confirmed password accounts and clears away unconfirmed ones. Emails are lowercased.

## What changes behind the scenes

- **#95:** a failed Google token refresh no longer writes the refresh token into CloudWatch. Every Google, GCS and Cloud Run error is logged as a scrubbed summary.
- **#91:** Google Analytics never receives share codes, ids or sign-in codes. The GA stream settings were turned off by hand.
- **#94:** a failed Create Timeline now emails the founder. Cancellations and refusals do not.
- **#3:** the renderer stops re-running a render it already marked failed, and still renders a job the stuck-job sweep failed before it ever started.
- **serverless.yml:** adds `AdminDeleteUser` and removes the unused `AdminDisableUser`. `FAILURE_ALERT_EMAIL` sends failure alerts to alerts@kindredreels.com.

Cloud changes already made by hand (recorded in INFRASTRUCTURE.md): the prod render queue has a dead-letter queue, dead-letter and DynamoDB alarms go to alerts@, and the open test services, Grafana copies and key, orphan queue and old face collections are gone.

## How it was checked

Each fix was built in isolation and reviewed by an independent agent. No review found a blocker, and every finding was fixed or recorded. Backend: 2,513 tests pass and lint is clean. Frontend: 1,621 tests pass, lint is clean and the build succeeds. Processing: 285 tests pass. An older flaky contributor-page test was fixed at the cause.

## After merge (dev deploys automatically)

1. Start a tribute on dev: the consent screen comes before reference photos.
2. Try a password signup on an email that signs in with Google: you get the "use Continue with Google" message.
3. Open a memory link: it lands on that memory, with no Browse All button.
4. After the next prod release: DebugView shows `/watch/[code]`, not the real code.

Plan and decisions: `.claude/plans/tier1-security-pass.md` (local). The remaining tier 1 work (SSH to SSM, scoped roles, callback tokens, monitoring, token encryption) is wave 2.

body:
This is the second batch of tier 1 work: exposure that affects people already using Kindred Reels. It adds a way for users to delete their account, lets the admin see everything in a project, fixes three admin and renderer bugs, and adds the code half of several cloud changes. Those cloud changes (alarms, narrower permissions) take effect only when they are applied by hand, one at a time, per the runbooks included here.

## What changes for people

- **Delete my account.** New Account page (click your name in the header). The button asks you to type DELETE, then everything is deleted in the background: every project and its media, face templates, music, feedback, Google connections (revoked at Google), then the sign-in itself. A confirmation email follows. A tab left open elsewhere cannot recreate the account afterwards. The privacy policy says both ways to delete.
- **Admins see everything.** The Library, the Not Included panel and voice memories on any project. Editing stays owner-only. One shared access rule, so the query-string routes cannot drift from the rest again.

## Fixes

- **Admin "disable user" works again.** PR #224 removed its Cognito permission after an unchecked claim that nothing used it.
- **Admin delete no longer times out on large accounts (#77).** It uses the same background path as the user button.
- **#99:** an email containing a quote or backslash can no longer change what the Cognito lookup matches.
- **#101:** a render that keeps failing is now marked failed and emails the founder on the third try. Before, the guard fired after five tries, but the dead-letter queue takes the job after three, so it never ran.
- **User music:** it is no longer dropped when an admin renders someone else's project.

## Groundwork (applied later, by hand, one yes each)

- **#84, signed callback tokens, stage 1.** The old password still works. Tokens start only once the new key secret exists, and the key is re-read every 10 minutes, so rotating it does not break jobs in flight. Runbook: `docs/runbooks/callback-tokens.md`.
- **Monitoring.** `GET /health/deep` reads the database. `infra/monitoring/` holds 16 prod alarms (API errors and slowness, worker errors, queue backlogs, the stuck-job sweep, failed timelines) plus a GCP script for uptime checks and Cloud Run alerts. Everything goes to alerts@kindredreels.com, for about $2.50 a month. Runbook: `infra/monitoring/RUNBOOK.md`.
- **#83 / #96, least privilege.** `infra/iam/` holds per-stage renderer roles and a per-service Cloud Run account plan. The renderer no longer needs a full-table scan to find music. Runbook: `infra/iam/RUNBOOK.md`.

## How it was checked

Each piece was built in isolation and reviewed by an independent agent. No review found a blocker, and every finding was fixed, including a key-rotation bug, a locked-but-never-deleted account case, and the music bug above. The combined branch passes backend lint and 2,670 tests, frontend lint and 1,636 tests on two runs, the build, and 302 processing tests.

## After merge (dev deploys automatically, including serverless.yml)

1. On dev, create a throwaway account, add a project, then delete the account from the Account page. You should be signed out and see the confirmation page, then get the email.
2. As admin, open another user's project on dev: Library, Not Included and voice memories all load.
3. Admin Users page on dev: disable a test user, then confirm they cannot sign in.

Still parked on their own branches until their cloud prerequisite exists: token encryption (#86, needs the KMS keys) and SSM deploys with CI's own AWS login (#82 #89 #90, needs the GitHub OIDC roles).

The two internal callback routes (clip analysis from Cloud Run, render
outcome from the EC2 renderer) used to accept one global password and then
trust whatever project and video ids the body named. Now the backend signs
each job's own ids with a new key when it dispatches the job, and the
callback accepts only a token that matches the ids in the body. The old
password is still accepted, compared in constant time, and every callback
logs CALLBACK_AUTH=token, legacy or rejected so the changeover can be
watched. Tokens are only minted once the new signing key secret exists, so
this is safe to deploy before the secret is created.

- shared/callbackAuth.js: mint and verify kr1.<exp>.<sig> tokens

  so Cloud Run needs no change
- createVideo stores a render token on the VIDEO# record; the renderer
  sends it and falls back to the old secret when it is absent

  embeddings included, and ignores clips naming another item
- render callback: emails only when the record really is complete (alert

Review fixes for the per-job callback tokens (#84). The key used to be cached
for the life of a container, so deleting or rotating it never reached warm
containers and a token minted in one container could fail in another. Now
every container re-reads the key every 10 minutes, whatever the last answer
was, and the verifier accepts the current key or the previous one (the
secret's AWSPREVIOUS version, else the key the container held before). A
failed read keeps the last known keys and waits like any other read, so a
failing Secrets Manager is not called on every request. A secret scheduled
for deletion reads as no key.

The runbook moves into the repo as docs/runbooks/callback-tokens.md, with
the rollback and rotation steps corrected to match.

body:
When someone connects Google Photos or YouTube, Google gives us a refresh token that keeps working until they revoke it. We stored those tokens as plain text on the user record, so anything that could read the table could reach those users' photos and channels. This PR encrypts them with a per-stage KMS key before storing them.

## What changes

- **Encryption.** `shared/tokenCrypto.js` encrypts each token with KMS and ties it to its user, provider and field. A value copied onto another record will not decrypt. Stored values look like `kms1:...`, and old plain-text values are still read, so nothing breaks before the migration.
- **Where tokens are read.** The user record no longer carries tokens at all, only a `connected` flag. Tokens are read through `getUserOAuthTokens`, which decrypts one field at a time.
- **Disconnect** now revokes the grant with the refresh token. Before, it used the usually-expired access token, so Google refused and the grant stayed live.
- **KMS failure** shows "try again in a few minutes". It never disconnects anyone silently.
- **Migration script** `backend/src/scripts/encryptStoredOAuthTokens.js`: dry-run by default, never prints values. It found 2 Google Photos connections and 1 YouTube connection to encrypt on dev.
- **Account deletion** (from #225) now reads tokens through the new decrypting reader. Combining the two branches would otherwise have quietly stopped it revoking Google access. Tests cover this.

## Keys (already created, 2026-09-24)

`alias/kindred-oauth-tokens-dev` and `-prod`, with yearly rotation. Only each stage's Lambda role can decrypt, and only for calls carrying the app's tag. The founder can decrypt with the dev key (for local development) but only encrypt with prod. No key policy delegates `CreateGrant`. All of this was checked with dummy data. The ARNs are in `serverless.yml`, and a test fails CI if a placeholder ever comes back.

## After merge

Dev deploys automatically. Then, per `infra/kms/RUNBOOK.md`:
1. On dev, connect Google Photos and run one import; connect YouTube if convenient. New tokens are stored encrypted.
2. Run the migration on dev with `--apply`, then confirm no plain text is left.
3. Prod release, then the same migration on prod.

Local `npm run dev` needs `OAUTH_TOKEN_KMS_KEY_ID=alias/kindred-oauth-tokens-dev` in `backend/.env` (Dimitri edits that file).

Checks: backend lint clean, 2,748 tests pass; frontend lint clean, 1,636 tests pass (no frontend changes).
